Alcott does not claim to cover every duty of a young woman's life. He picks those he felt other writers slighted, above all temperance, meaning self-control in all things.

Chapters urge care for health, good habits, sound friendships, and a useful, steady life at home and in the world. The advice now reads as old-fashioned, yet it shows plainly what middle-class America taught its daughters. Historians and general readers alike can learn much from its earnest, practical tone.
9183-wilfrid-cumbermede:
George MacDonald wrote this tale of a boy, a sword, and a haunted house, told in the first person. Wilfrid finds himself with an uncle and aunt, climbs a chimney stair, and meets a pendulum, a ghost, and lessons at school. A sword on the wall and a loss at Moldwarp Hall shape his youth.

Later chapters take him to an ice cave, the mountains, and Oxford, with Charley nursing him after a mishap. MacDonald mixes adventure with moral growth. The book still pleases as a boy's story with depth, wonder, and a strong sense of place.
9299-italian-letters-vols-i-and-ii-or-th:
William Godwin wrote this epistolary novel as Italian Letters, or the history of the Count de St. Julian, edited with an introduction by Burton Pollin. Volume One opens in Palermo, where the Count writes to the Marquis of Pescara on his father's death. He scorns fashionable forms of condolence, praising instead honest grief.

His friend Rinaldo, heir to fortune and title, weeps an unaffected tear, unspoiled by flattery. Letters trace love, honor, and Italian society through St. Julian's eyes. The novel remains an early Godwin work, formal, feeling, and rich in eighteenth-century manners.
9814-the-poetical-works-of-mark-akenside:
George Gilfillan edited The Poetical Works of Mark Akenside, opening with a life of the poet. Akenside, born at Newcastle in 1721 to a butcher father and Mary Lumsden, was baptized among Presbyterian Dissenters. Gilfillan notes the oddity of a butcher's shop birthing The Pleasures of Imagination, then cites like cases: Kirke White and others of humble trade. No decent calling, he argues, bars genius.

The volume pairs Akenside's poems, chiefly The Pleasures of Imagination, with Gilfillan's memoir. Akenside's verse favors lofty meditation on taste and fancy. A reader gets a Victorian edition of an eighteenth-century poet, with a life that defends humble birth.
a-boy-s-ride: Gulielma Zollinger tells a boys adventure of a ride through peril and pursuit. Its young hero seeks shelter within castle walls, finds guides and friends, and hides among oak trees and reeds. Illustrations follow scenes of flight, capture, and narrow escape across the countryside. The story mixes history and daring in a tale meant for young readers.
a-declaration-of-the-causes-which-mooved: Queen Elizabeth the First declares the causes that moved her navy's chief commanders on their voyage for Portugal. On June 30, 1589, English ships arrested vessels of corn and war provisions bound for Lisbon in the service of the King of Spain. The declaration justifies the seizure as an act of war at sea. It stands as a plain Tudor state paper on naval power and trade.
a-question-of-latitude:
Richard Harding Davis follows Everett, a young magazine writer known for honest attacks on graft and corruption. His editors trust him because no one has caught him in exaggeration or unfair play. Sent south on an assignment, Everett finds that the rules he lives by sit oddly in a hot, slow country where men do business differently.

The tale tests his code against local custom, a shady consul, and his own pride. Davis, a famous reporter of his day, writes with pace and clean detail. The story asks whether right and wrong shift with the climate, or whether a man must carry his own weather with him.
a-versailles-christmas-tide: Mary Stuart Boyd spends a Christmas-tide at Versailles in this 1901 volume, with fifty-three illustrations by A. S. Boyd. The contents run from the unexpected happening and Ogams through the town, the Christmas tree, New Year's Day, and ice-bound days to a haunted chateau, Marie Antoinette, and prisoners released. Illustrations of the summons, storm warnings, treasure trove, chestnuts in the avenue, and snow in the park accompany a holiday abroad.
abraham-lincoln-an-horatian-ode: Richard Henry Stoddard mourns Abraham Lincoln in an Horatian ode, published at New York in 1865. The title page records Lincoln born February 12, 1809, and assassinated on Good Friday, April 14, 1865. Epigraphs from Shakespeare cry confusion's masterpiece, sacrilegious murder breaking open the Lord's anointed temple, and an alarum bell ringing murder and treason. The ode answers assassination with classical measure and public grief.
adam-bede:
George Eliot's first full novel is set in the farming parish of Hayslope and organized in six books, as the contents show. The title figure, Adam Bede, is a skilled carpenter. Around him gather his brother Seth and the Methodist preacher Dinah Morris. The Poysers of the Hall Farm and Hetty Sorrel complete the circle. Hetty is the dairy maid whose beauty governs her small world.

Chapter titles trace the arc. They run from the preaching on the green and evenings in the wood to a birthday feast, a crisis, and a hidden dread. Then come a journey in despair, the tidings, a trial, a verdict, and hours in a prison cell. Hetty's fall through the young squire Arthur Donnithorne brings the catastrophe. Dinah's steadiness and Adam's slow forgiving close the book at a harvest supper and marriage bells.
aikenside:
Mary Jane Holmes lists her earlier novels on the title page. Maggie Miller, Lena Rivers, English Orphans, and Tempest and Sunshine stand among them. The book then opens in Devonshire. The good people there are quarreling about the minister and his wife. A school examination brings young Madeline Clyde before the examining committee, and her life changes with its result.

Twenty-four chapters follow Maddy through convalescence, a generous letter, life at Aikenside with the proud family there, holidays, a growing burden, and the interval before a marriage. Holmes was among the most widely read American novelists of her century, writing domestic tales of love, class, and conscience for an audience that bought her books by the hundred thousand.
an-essay-on-the-american-contribution-an:
Winston Churchill's An Essay on the American Contribution and the Democratic Idea argues that idealism is the American's ruling trait. Emerson and William James, he says, proclaimed it first. He quotes Firmin Roz's Sorbonne address on American idealism with approval. Europe mistook Americans for money grabbers whose philosophy is the dollar.

The essay marches through the national record: colonists animated by an ideal, a constitution ahead of its age, and democracy established in practice. Churchill confesses the failures frankly — Florida seized, Texas annexed, Mexico fought without unmixed pride. The war with Spain in 1898, fought to liberate Cuba, marks for him a transition in international ethics. America's contribution is an idea tested by its own betrayals. Written amid the Great War, the essay calls the republic back to its mission: democracy as a gift to be kept by being given.
an-international-episode:
Henry James wrote this novella about two young Englishmen who cross to America in the summer of 1874, as the opening pages state. Lord Lambeth and his friend Percy Beaumont land in a sweltering New York, ride up Broadway in a high coach, and find the bright, crowded city very odd. Their travels carry them to Newport, where American leisure society is on display.

There the young lord falls in with Bessie Alden, a quick, independent Boston girl, and an attraction grows that neither family quite approves. James builds the comedy from small collisions of manners: English reserve against American frankness, title against money, old assumptions against new ones. The tale is an early, light version of the international theme James returned to all his life.
britannica-1911-abode:
Abode receives a law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. The word, from abide, to dwell or wait, means in general a dwelling. English law narrows it below domicile: the place of a man's residence or business, fixed or passing.

Business can supply the abode though the man sleeps elsewhere, making the term looser than residence, defined in one case as where a man lives with family and sleeps at night. A solicitor's office stands as his abode for serving a notice of action. Public Health Act service at a place of business likewise holds good. Cases of 1835 and 1852 anchor the rulings, giving the small word a firm legal edge.
britannica-1911-accolade:
Accolade was the ceremony used in conferring knighthood, its name drawn from a word for the neck. The 1911 Britannica entry admits scholars disagree whether the original act was an embrace or a slight blow on the neck or cheek, since both customs are ancient. Gregory of Tours describes early French kings kissing new knights on the left cheek while giving the gilt shoulder-belt.

Blows softened over time. A blow with the naked fist, a real box on the ear, gave way to a gentle stroke with the flat of a sword on the neck or shoulders. British sovereigns still use that form when conferring knighthood. The word also names a brace joining staves in printed music.
britannica-1911-acosta-jose-de:
Jose de Acosta (about 1539-1600) was a Spanish Jesuit author. He was born at Medina del Campo. He joined the Jesuits in 1551. In 1571 the order sent him to Peru. He served as provincial there for five years. In 1583 he published a catechism in Quichua and Aymara. It was the first book printed in Peru. He returned to Spain in 1587. Opposition to his superior led to imprisonment. Later posts took him to Valladolid and Salamanca.

Writing made his lasting name. His Historia natural y moral de las Indias appeared in 1590. Translations into six languages followed quickly. Early books treat general questions of the New World. Middle books cover the physical geography of Mexico and Peru. Their natural history gets full treatment too. Final books describe native religion and government.
britannica-1911-acuna-christoval-de:
Christoval de Acuna (1597-about 1676) was a Spanish missionary and explorer. He was born at Burgos and became a Jesuit in 1612. Mission work took him to Chile and Peru. He rose to rector of the college of Cuenca. In 1639 he joined Pedro Texeira's Amazon expedition. His task was scientific observation for Spain's government. He was to draw up the official report.

Ten months of travel produced his narrative. He prepared it while awaiting a ship in Peru. Philip IV received the author coldly, tradition says. The king even tried to suppress the book. Portugal had just revolted from Spain. Madrid feared Lisbon would profit from Amazon intelligence. His New Discovery of the Great River of the Amazons appeared in 1641 anyway.
britannica-1911-albornoz-gil-alvarez-de:
Albornoz, Gil Alvarez de, a Spanish cardinal born at Cuenca early in the fourteenth century, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His mother came from the Luna family, and his uncle was archbishop of Toledo. Educated at Saragossa and trained in law at Toulouse, he rose early through family influence. He became archdeacon of Calatrava and a member of the king's council while still young.

In 1337 Albornoz succeeded his uncle as archbishop of Toledo. He fought in person at Tarifa in 1340 against a great invasion from Africa and led his archbishopric's levy at Algeciras in 1344. A mission to Pope Clement VI at Avignon showed his diplomatic skill, and the pope made him cardinal in 1350. Sent to Italy as legate, he worked to restore papal authority in the states of the Church. Astute with men and an effective fighter, he paved the way for Urban V's return to Rome in 1362.
britannica-1911-alcalde:
Judging sits at the root of the Spanish title alcalde, a word taken from the Arabic al-quadi, the Cadi or judge. Every use of the title keeps some trace of that court role. An alcalde de corte judged cases at the palace court, with sway in and around the king's home.

Town life gave the word its lasting sense. A mayor of a town or village who also did the work of a justice of the peace was an alcalde, and that, the entry notes, is now the title's sole meaning. The post is filled by vote each year, and in Spain men have often found it a thankless one. Readers must not mix alcalde up with alcaide. That word springs from a separate Arabic term for a commander and means the man who governs a fortress.
britannica-1911-almagro-diego-de: Peru's conquest bound the Spanish commander Diego de Almagro (1475–1538) to Pizarro, first as partner and then as rival. He was born at Aldea del Rey, though one account calls him a foundling from the village that gave him his name. At Panama in 1525 he joined Pizarro and Hernando de Luque in their scheme. Their quarrel over territory ended with Pizarro ordering his execution in 1538.
britannica-1911-almeida-dom-francisco-de:
Death found Dom Francisco de Almeida (c. 1450–1510), Portuguese India's first viceroy, far from India, near the site of Cape Town. Stopping for water on 1 March 1510, he was killed in a fight with local people. Lisbon-born, he was the seventh son of the second count of Abrantes and came from one of Portugal's most honoured families. As a youth he fought under Ferdinand of Aragon in the Moorish wars of 1485 to 1492.

March 1505 brought his appointment as viceroy and a large fleet to command. Quiloa fell to him with little struggle; Mombasa he destroyed after stiff resistance. Forts rose at Angediva and Cannanore, a trade treaty was made with Malacca, and he ruled from Cochin. His son Lorenzo, serving under him, likely reached Ceylon before any other Portuguese, while another of his captains sighted Madagascar.
britannica-1911-arcade:
Arcade, in architecture, is a range of arches. Columns or piers support those arches. Church naves use arcades to separate aisles. Cloisters use them around covered walks. The Ducal Palace at Venice shows them famously. St Mark's Square shows them too. Italian palace courts display them commonly. Paris has them at the Palais-Royal. The Place des Vosges offers another example.

Rome holds the earliest known examples. The Tabularium is one such building. The theatre of Marcellus is another. The Colosseum completes the Roman trio. Diocletian's palace at Spalato shows a variant. Its arches rest directly on capitals. No entablature intervenes in that design. Decorative galleries on church façades count too. Blind arcades form part of the wall itself. Shopping passages took the name later. Burlington Arcade in London exemplifies that sense.
britannica-1911-avila-y-zuniga-luis-de:
Avila y Zuniga, Luis de (c. 1490-c. 1560), was a Spanish historian born at Placentia. Probably of low origin, he married a wealthy heiress of the Zuniga family and added her name to his own. He rose fast in the favor of the emperor Charles V.

Avila served as ambassador to Rome and became grand commander of the order of the Knights of Alcantara. He went with Charles to Africa in 1541 and served in the war of the league of Schmalkalden. His history of that war, printed in 1548, won wide fame and translation into five languages. The entry warns that his closeness to Charles makes the book strongly partial, its misrepresentations sharply criticized.
britannica-1911-aviles-pedro-menendez-de:
Avilés, Pedro Menéndez de (1519-1574), was a Spanish seaman and founder of St Augustine, Florida, born at Avilés in Asturias, one of nineteen children of a gentry family. At fourteen he ran away to sea and spent sixteen years as a corsair.

In 1549 Charles V set him to clear French pirates from Spain's north coast and the Canaries. From 1554 he commanded the flota, the convoy carrying trade between Spain and America, refusing bribes and guarding treasure so well that the emperor approved him warmly. The trade board, the Casa de Contratacion, hated his high-handed ways and had him jailed for twenty months on unknown charges before royal orders freed him. The entry's opening line credits him with founding St Augustine.
britannica-1911-ayala-don-pedro-lopez-de:
Ayala, Don Pedro Lopez de (1332-1407), was a Spanish statesman, historian, and poet born at Vittoria. He rose at the court of Peter the Cruel. He finally left that king's cause. In later campaigns he fought with honor. Twice he fell prisoner. The Black Prince took him in 1367, and the Portuguese took him in 1385.

Favored by Henry II and John I of Castile, Ayala became grand chancellor of the realm in 1398 under Henry III. His chief works are chronicles of the four Castilian kings of his lifetime, mostly scenes he witnessed himself, and so generally accurate. He also wrote a long satirical, teaching poem picturing his own experience and the morals of his age. He died at Calahorra in 1407.
britannica-1911-ayala-y-herrera-adelardo:
Ayala y Herrera, Adelardo Lopez de (1828-1879), was a Spanish writer and politician born at Guadalcanal, where he began writing plays for the town theatre as a boy. His early pieces were played by men only, since travelling companies never came and ladies did not act there.

At Seville university his studies were undistinguished, but playwright Garcia Gutierrez encouraged his stage ambitions. Settling in Madrid in 1850 with no friends or influence, he won the Teatro Español with a verse play in 1851 and made his name at once. Rioja, from 1854, was held his finest work. Government posts, party shifts from Moderates to Progressives, and campaign journalism in El Padre Cobos filled the same busy years.
britannica-1911-ayllon-lucas-vasquez-de:
Ayllon, Lucas Vasquez de (c. 1475-1526), was a Spanish adventurer and colonizer in America, born probably at Toledo. He sailed to Hispaniola with Ovando in 1502, served as magistrate in its towns, sat on its high court, and grew rich in trade.

Turning to the North American mainland, Ayllon sent Gordillo exploring in 1521 and won a charter from Charles V in 1523 to plant colonies. In 1526 he sailed himself with 500 colonists and about 100 African slaves, an early use of slave labor in what became the United States. His town of San Miguel, near the Pedee river by most accounts, sickened with fever; Ayllon died that October, slaves rose, and the survivors abandoned the place.
britannica-1911-azara-don-jose-nicholas-:
Azara, Don Jose Nicholas de (1731-1804), was a Spanish diplomatist born at Barbunales in Aragon, made Spanish agent and procurator-general in 1765 and ambassador at Rome in 1785. Long resident there, he collected Italian antiquities, patronized art, and played a leading, risky part in expelling the Jesuits from Spain.

Azara helped secure the election of Pius VI and served the pope through exile and death after France took Rome in 1798. As ambassador in Paris his government forced him to negotiate the treaty of San Ildefonso, which subjected Spain wholly to Napoleon, a master he personally liked. He died worn out in Paris in 1804, embittered, the entry says, by seeing what the French alliance would cost his country. His younger brother Felix won fame studying South American nature and boundaries.
britannica-1911-azoimide:
Azoimide, or hydrazoic acid, is a compound of nitrogen and hydrogen first isolated by Curtius in 1890. The entry walks through his route to it: benzoyl compounds treated with hydrazine, then nitrous acid, then boiled with alkali to free salts of the new acid.

An improved path runs through hippuric acid and its hydrazine derivative, ending with distillation of the sodium salt with dilute sulphuric acid. The pure acid is a colourless liquid of very unpleasant smell, boiling near room heat and extremely explosive. Its water solution attacks metals like zinc and iron, forming salts called azides, all of them explosive. In behavior it resembles the halogen acids, giving poorly soluble salts with lead, silver, and mercury.
britannica-1911-azurara-gomes-eannes-de:
Azurara, Gomes Eannes de ( ?-1474), was the second notable Portuguese chronicler, who came to letters in middle life and joined the royal library under Fernão Lopes during King Duarte's reign. By 1452 he held sole charge of it, and in 1454 he succeeded Lopes as chief keeper of the archives and royal chronicler.

His Chronicle of the Discovery and Conquest of Guinea was drafted by 1453. It is the standing authority for the early Portuguese voyages down Africa's coast. Prince Henry the Navigator sponsored those voyages. The chronicle also sketches Henry's life work. Royal commissions took him even to Africa for a year gathering material. The entry praises his labor and accuracy, while noting his court post kept him from telling the whole truth about his hero, Henry.
britannica-1911-bachaumont-louis-petit-d:
Bachaumont, Louis Petit de (1690-1771), was a French writer of noble family. He was brought up at the Versailles court. He passed his whole life in Paris. There he centred the salon of Madame Doublet de Persan. There, talk about art and books took the form of lively, malicious gossip.

The salon kept a news register dealing largely in scandal and in books the censor had suppressed. Bachaumont's name clings to its first volumes, published anonymously as Secret Memoirs for the History of the Republic of Letters, though his exact share is disputed. Others carried it to thirty-six volumes by 1779. The entry values the work as a historical source, above all for the banned literature of the age.
britannica-1911-balance-of-trade:
Balance of trade is an old term from the age of the mercantile theory, when trade was judged by how much gold and silver a country took in. The 1911 Britannica entry traces that view and the common belief that a surplus of precious metals meant profit for the nation.

Adam Smith's reply, that gold and silver are goods like any others, sits at the core of the piece. The entry then turns to modern talk of imports and exports, and to claims that an excess of imports is bad and an excess of exports is good. It tests those claims rather than taking them on trust.
britannica-1911-balboa-vasco-nunez-de:
Vasco Nuñez de Balboa (about 1475–1517) was a Spanish explorer of America, famed as the man who first reached the Pacific from the New World. Born at Jerez de los Caballeros, he sailed in 1501 with Rodrigo de Bastidas, then tried farming on Hispaniola and fell into debt.

In 1510 he joined Enciso's relief voyage, by some accounts hidden in a cask, and reached the ruined post of San Sebastian. The 1911 Britannica entry tells how he urged a move to Darien, helped found Santa Maria de la Antigua, and rose to lead the colony. From Darien he pushed inland toward the far sea he had heard of.
britannica-1911-baliol-john-de:
John de Baliol (1249–1315) was a king of Scotland. He was a son of John de Baliol of Barnard Castle and of Dervorguila, heiress of Galloway. On his elder brother's death in 1278 he became head of the family, with wide lands in England, France, and Scotland.

He came to notice in 1290, when the Scottish throne fell vacant on the death of Margaret, the Maid of Norway. Baliol claimed the crown through his mother's line from David, earl of Huntingdon. His chief rival was Robert Bruce. The 1911 Britannica entry tells how Edward I of England was called in to judge the claim, and first demanded to be owned as overlord of Scotland.
britannica-1911-balsham-hugh-de:
Hugh de Balsham (died 1286) was an English churchman, first noted as sub-prior of the monastery of Ely. When Bishop William of Kilkenny died in 1256, the Ely monks chose Hugh as bishop, against the wishes of Henry III, who had given the see's revenues to another man. The pope confirmed the choice in 1257.

Hugh set about repairing the harm done to the diocese. His lasting work came at Cambridge. In 1280 a charter let him swap the lay brethren of his hospital of St John for studious scholars. A second charter four years later set those scholars apart, and for them he founded and endowed Peterhouse. The 1911 Britannica entry keeps that founding as the core of his fame.
britannica-1911-balustrade:
Balustrade names a parapet or low screen made of a rail or coping held up on balusters, the small posts treated in the entry just before this one. It can guard a stair, a balcony, or a roof edge. The 1911 Britannica entry is brief and keeps to the forms the feature takes.

Sometimes a balustrade is purely decorative, set below the sill of a window that does not reach the ground. Sometimes carved foliage takes the place of the rail. Other so-called balustrades are made of upright stone slabs, pierced with open work. The entry points to the Ca' d'Oro at Venice and to the balconies of the minarets at Cairo as cases in point.
britannica-1911-balzac-honore-de:
Honoré de Balzac (1799–1850) was a French novelist, born at Tours on 20 May 1799. His father rose in army supply and hospital posts after the Revolution. Yet he had no real right to the name Balzac at all. The family name was Balssa, borne by day labourers and small peasants in the Tarn. Honoré himself added the de only after 1830.

The 1911 Britannica entry, a long one, opens with that family history and the novelist's two sisters and younger brother, then follows his life and work in full. His mother, an heiress of strong faculty, outlived him. Laure, the elder sister and his favourite, later wrote his life, a fact the entry notes at the start.
britannica-1911-balzac-jean-louis-guez-d:
Jean Louis Guez de Balzac (1594–1654) was a French author, born at Angoulême in 1594. At eighteen he travelled in Holland with Théophile de Viaud, a friend who later became a bitter foe in print. The duc d'Épernon and his son, Cardinal de la Valette, backed him early and took him to Rome.

Letters made his name. His Lettres of 1624, written to friends and to great men at court, won wide praise. They earned him a place at the Hôtel de Rambouillet. Richelieu, though, never gave him the office he hoped for. Elected to the Academy in 1634, he kept up his letters from his château. The 1911 Britannica entry faults their empty, affected matter but credits their style with bringing new clearness and precision to French prose.
britannica-1911-barricade:
Barricade, also spelled barricado, is defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as a makeshift defence thrown up in a hurry. The word comes from the Spanish barricada, from barrica, a cask, because casks filled with earth were used early on to build such barriers. A barricade could be made of earth, paving stones, trees, or anything else close at hand that would slow an enemy down.

Street fighting is the use the entry stresses most. Barricades were most often raised across a street to block an advance. The word had a second, naval sense as well. On old wooden warships it named a fence or rail across the quarter-deck, held up by posts and strengthened with other material. That rail gave the crew some protection while the ship was in action.
britannica-1911-barthelemy-anatole-jean-:
Anatole Jean-Baptiste Antoine de Barthélemy (1821–1904), a French archaeologist and numismatist born at Reims, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. Numismatics, the study of coins, is the field that made his name. He also worked on Brittany, publishing studies of the Breton revolution in 1858 and a large six-volume history of the old Breton bishoprics, with their monuments, between 1855 and 1879.

Coins dominate the list of his books. Barthélemy wrote popular manuals on ancient coinage and on medieval and modern coinage, both later revised, plus many technical papers in journals. Named studies cover Merovingian coinage, the Parisian coinage, and the origin of the tournois coinage, and he edited the numismatics volume for a national historical committee. Election to the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-lettres came in 1897. A note on his younger brother Édouard's work on the old French nobility closes the entry.
britannica-1911-barthelemy-francois-marq:
François Barthélemy, marquis de Barthélemy (1747 or 1750–1830), a French politician, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Trained for diplomacy by his uncle, the abbé Jean Jacques Barthélemy, he served as secretary of legation in Sweden, Switzerland, and England. As minister in Switzerland he negotiated the treaties of Basel with Prussia and Spain in 1795, the agreements that took those powers out of the war against France.

High office brought sudden ruin. Elected to the Directory in May 1797 with royalist support, Barthélemy was arrested in the Fructidor coup that September and deported to French Guiana. He escaped, reached England by way of the United States, and returned after Brumaire to sit in the senate. He helped establish the consulship for life and the empire, then abandoned Napoleon in 1814, became a peer of France, and received his marquis title after the second Restoration.
britannica-1911-bassompierre-francois-de:
François de Bassompierre (1579–1646), a French courtier born at the castle of Harrouel in Lorraine, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His old family had served the dukes of Burgundy and Lorraine. Presented at Henry IV's court in 1598, he became a great favourite, sharing fully in court pleasures. He campaigned in Savoy and Hungary, backed the royalists against Marie de' Medici's party, and won a marshal's baton in the Huguenot rising of 1621–1622.

Diplomacy served Bassompierre badly, and suspicion ended his career. Missions to Madrid, Switzerland, and London all proved fruitless. Implicated slightly in the 1630 plot against Richelieu, he was arrested in 1631. He stayed in the Bastille until Richelieu's death freed him in 1643. His offices were then restored, but he lived quietly in Normandy until 1646. His Mémoires, published in 1665, remain an important source for his time.
britannica-1911-bassville-nicolas-jean-h:
Nicolas Jean Hugon de Bassville (1753–1793), a French journalist and diplomat born at Abbeville, is the subject of a dramatic 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. Trained for the priesthood, he moved to Paris, published a mythology handbook in 1784, tutored two young Americans through Berlin, and knew Mirabeau. At the Revolution he edited the Mercure international. He then entered diplomacy under Lebrun-Tondu, going to Naples and, unofficially, to Rome.

Provocation in Rome cost Bassville his life. He posed as protector of Rome's extreme Jacobins, demanded the expulsion of French émigrés, and replaced the embassy's fleur-de-lys with a picture of Liberty. His insults to the papal secretary enraged the Roman crowd. In a riot on 13 January 1793 he was dragged from his carriage and so roughly handled that he died. France magnified the affair into a papal murder of its representative. The treaty of Tolentino later won his family compensation.
britannica-1911-bastide:
Bastide, from a Provençal word for building, names the fortified new towns founded in south-western France in the Middle Ages, as explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They match the villes neuves of northern France. Abbeys, nobles, and the crown founded them, often two authorities together. A bastide served as a defensive post and as a centre of population for thinly settled districts, while bringing its founders revenue and power in return.

Plan and charter define the type. Founders conceded liberal charters to attract settlers. The towns were built on a rectangular plan, with a large central square and straight streets at right angles. Monpazier in the Dordogne, founded by the English in 1284, is the surviving example the entry picks out. Mont-de-Marsan, the oldest bastide, dates from 1141, and the founding movement ran through the twelfth to fourteenth centuries, peaking between 1250 and 1350.
britannica-1911-batarnay-imbert-de:
Imbert de Batarnay (about 1438–1523), a French statesman from an old but little-known family of Dauphiné, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A chance link brought him to the dauphin Louis in 1455, when the prince was in arms against his father. Batarnay joined him and followed him into exile in Burgundy. When Louis became king as Louis XI, he heaped gifts on his loyal man: a rich wife, estates, and high posts at court.

Trust kept Batarnay busy for four reigns. He watched the duke of Guienne's plots, shielded Roussillon from the king's wrath, and met Edward IV of England at Picquigny. Charles VIII kept him in close service, and he guarded the dauphin during the Naples war. Louis XII used him against Genoa, and Francis I made him governor to the dauphin in 1518. He died in May 1523.
britannica-1911-bazire-claude:
Claude Bazire (1764–1794) was a French revolutionary, deputy for the Côte d’Or in the Legislative Assembly. He made his name by attacking the court and the “Austrian committee” of the Tuileries. In June 1792 he spoke for removing the king from the throne.

In the Convention Bazire sat with the Mountain, opposed any delay in the trial of Louis XVI, and voted for his death. He joined the attack on the Girondists, yet as a member of the committee of general security he spoke against the Terror. Caught up in Chabot’s East India Company forgery case, he was tried beside Danton and executed in April 1794.
britannica-1911-bellarmine-roberto-franc:
Roberto Francesco Romolo Bellarmine (1542–1621) was an Italian cardinal and theologian born at Monte Pulciano in Tuscany. His father planned a political career for him, but he felt called to the priesthood and joined the Society of Jesus in 1560. He taught Greek at Mondovi while still a student.

At Louvain from 1569 Bellarmine lectured on theology and was forced by debate on grace and free will to sharpen his own positions. Called to Rome in 1576, he took the new chair of controversial theology at the Roman College. Those lectures grew into his famed Disputationes, the great Jesuit answer to Protestant teaching of the age.
britannica-1911-bellegarde:
Bellegarde is the name of a noted French family, the house of Saint-Lary. Roger de Saint-Lary, baron of Bellegarde, fought with distinction in the wars against the French Protestants. Henry III loaded him with favours and made him marshal of France, yet he fell from grace and died by poison in 1579.

His nephew Roger de Saint-Lary de Termes stood high with three kings in turn, Henry III, Henry IV and Louis XIII. As royal master of the horse and governor of Burgundy, he saw his estate of Seurre raised in 1619 to a duchy named Bellegarde. The title later moved to Choisy-aux-Loges, passed to the Pardaillan de Gondrin family, and at Seurre was borne by the princes of Condé.
britannica-1911-belloy-dormont-de:
Dormont de Belloy was the stage name of Pierre Laurent Buirette (1727–1775), a French dramatist born at Saint-Flour. Trained for the law by his uncle, a Paris advocate, he hated the work and ran off with a troupe of actors playing at northern courts. His uncle blocked his play Titus in Paris for years.

After his guardian died, de Belloy came home and scored with Zelmire in 1762. Le Siège de Calais followed in 1765, a patriotic piece that fed on France’s shame in the Seven Years’ War and thrilled the public, though Diderot and Voltaire doubted its art. He entered the Academy in 1772, but no later play matched that success.
britannica-1911-benserade-isaac-de:
Isaac de Benserade (1613–1691) was a French poet born in Paris, baptised in November 1613. His family had ties to Richelieu, who granted him a pension of six hundred livres. He began with the tragedy Cléopâtre in 1635, followed by four other indifferent plays.

When Richelieu died the pension went, but Benserade rose at court all the same, writing words for the court ballets and entering the Academy in 1674. His fame today hangs on one piece: the sonnet on Job of 1651. Set against Voiture’s Urania, it split the court into two camps, Jobelins and Uranists, who argued the two poems’ merits for years. He spent his last years at Chantilly translating the Psalms.
britannica-1911-benzaldehyde:
Benzaldehyde, known in trade as oil of bitter almonds, is the simplest of the aromatic aldehydes, a family of sharp-smelling compounds. It was first isolated in 1803 and was studied closely by Liebig in 1837. In nature it sits inside amygdalin, a sugar-bound form found in bitter almonds, cherries, peaches and cherry laurel leaves.

Acids breaking amygdalin down set benzaldehyde free, and an enzyme does the same work inside the almond itself. Chemists make it many other ways: from benzyl alcohol, from benzoate salts, or straight from benzene by set reactions. The long technical entry then works through its properties and the many compounds it forms, down to its use in building quinoline dyes and drugs.
britannica-1911-beriot-charles-auguste-d:
Charles Auguste de Bériot (1802–1870) was a Belgian violinist and composer. He was never formally a pupil of Viotti or of Baillot, yet both men’s playing shaped his own. Concert tours brought him great success across Europe in his early career.

Courts in Belgium and France gave Bériot appointments, and from 1843 to 1852 he taught the violin at the Brussels conservatoire. Then his eyesight failed, and in 1858 he went blind. His compositions are still played, the entry notes. They are judged good, clean displays of technique, pieces that show a player’s art plainly rather than hiding it. The notice is brief: masters by influence, tours, a chair, blindness, and the works left behind.
britannica-1911-bernard-charles-de:
Charles de Bernard (1804–1850), born Pierre Marie Charles de Bernard du Grail de la Villette at Besançon, was a French novelist encouraged by Balzac, whose Peau de chagrin he had reviewed. After law and journalism he settled in Paris to write, and this 1911 Britannica entry surveys the fiction that followed.

His books picture provincial society and the Paris bourgeoisie. Gerfaut (1838) is named his masterpiece, and Le Nœud gordien (1838) held a story Sardou later turned into a comedy. Other titles include Les Ailes d'Icare, La Peau du lion, and Le Gentilhomme campagnard. His complete works filled twelve volumes after his death.
britannica-1911-bernard-claude:
Claude Bernard (1813–1878), the French physiologist, was born near Villefranche and reached medicine by an odd road, first writing plays in his spare hours as a druggist's assistant. This 1911 Britannica biography follows his move to Paris, his post under Magendie at the Collège de France, and his succession to Magendie's chair in 1855.

His central finding concerned the liver: besides secreting bile, it prepares sugar from the blood passing through it, a result that bears on the cause of diabetes. His lectures filled seventeen volumes, and his Introduction à la médecine expérimentale (1865) set out his method. Napoleon III, after meeting him, funded his laboratory.
britannica-1911-bernis-francois-joachim-:
François Joachim de Pierre de Bernis (1715–1794) was a French cardinal and statesman. He came from a noble but poor family at St Marcel-d'Ardèche. A younger son, he was meant for the church. At the court of Louis XV he won fame as an epigram writer. Madame de Pompadour gained him rooms in the Tuileries and a pension. In 1751 he went as envoy to Venice.

The 1911 Britannica entry follows his part in the talks before the Seven Years' War. He backed the Austrian alliance only as a short expedient. Colleagues overruled him, and he became foreign secretary. His poems, the entry judges, have no merit. His memoirs and letters of 1715 to 1758 still interest historians, it adds.
britannica-1911-biggleswade:
Biggleswade is a market town in Bedfordshire, England, 41 miles north by west of London. The Great Northern railway serves it. The 1911 Britannica entry gives 5,120 people in the urban district in 1901. The town lies on the east bank of the Ivel, a tributary of the Ouse. Flat fields around it grow vegetables for the London markets. The town is the centre of that trade.

It is an ancient borough by prescription, yet it never sent members to parliament. At Edward the Confessor's time Archbishop Stigand held the manor. Henry I granted it to the bishop of Lincoln, under whom the borough grew. Its spot on the Roman road north made it a farm centre early. Edward III renewed its Monday market licence in 1335. Straw-plaiting and lace making once employed the town, the entry adds.
britannica-1911-biron-armand-de-gontaut-:
Armand de Gontaut, Baron de Biron (1524–1592), was a celebrated French soldier of the 16th century. His family took its name from Biron in Périgord, where their castle still stands. As a page of the queen of Navarre he caught Marshal Brissac's eye. He saw active service in Italy under Brissac. An early wound left him lame for life, yet he stayed in arms. By 1557 he commanded in Guise's light horse.

At Dreux, St Denis, Jarnac, and Moncontour he served the royal cause with distinction. In 1569 he became a privy councillor and grand master of artillery. He led the royal forces at the siege of La Rochelle in 1572. In 1576 he was made a marshal of France. The 1911 Britannica article then continues with a later Biron, a revolutionary general. That descendant was guillotined on 31 December 1793 after the Vendée campaign.
britannica-1911-blainville-henri-marie-d:
Henri Marie Ducrotay de Blainville (1777–1850) was a French naturalist who followed Cuvier and Lamarck in the great Paris chairs. Born at Arques near Dieppe, he went to Paris about 1796 to study painting, then turned to natural history. Cuvier took notice of him and sometimes let him lecture in his place.

With Cuvier's help he gained the Paris chair of anatomy and zoology in 1812, though the two men later fell into open enmity. In 1830 he followed Lamarck in the museum chair of natural history, and in 1832 he took Cuvier's own chair of comparative anatomy, holding it for eighteen years. His long list of works runs from animal classification to a French fauna.
britannica-1911-boigne-benoit-de:
Benoît de Boigne (1751–1830) was a Savoyard soldier who built European-style armies for the Maratha ruler Mahadji Sindhia in India. Born at Chambéry, a fur merchant's son, he joined the French Irish Brigade in 1768, later served Russia, and was held by the Turks. Tales of Indian wealth then drew him east.

After brief East India Company service he joined Sindhia in 1784 to train his troops in European methods. His battalions held the field at Lalsot and Chaksana and won Agra in 1788, Patan and Merta in 1790, and Lakhairi in 1793. He rose to command Sindhia's whole army, stayed loyal after his patron's death, and sailed home in 1796 with a fortune of £400,000.
britannica-1911-boisrobert-francois-le-m:
François le Metel de Boisrobert (1592–1662) was a French poet and court wit who helped Cardinal Richelieu found the French Academy. Born at Caen and trained for the law, he practised at Rouen, then reached the Paris court by 1623 through a share in a Louvre ballet. Missions took him to England in 1625 and Rome in 1630.

Richelieu took to his humour and storytelling and made him one of the five poets who worked up the cardinal's own drama ideas. Boisrobert took orders and grew rich on church posts, yet his loose living brought repeated disgrace. He stayed generous to poorer writers, the entry notes. It was his suggestion that set Richelieu on the plan of the Academy, where he was an early, busy member.
britannica-1911-boissy-d-anglas-francois:
François Antoine de Boissy d'Anglas (1756–1828) was a French statesman of the Revolution who steered a middle course. Well schooled and literary at first, he bought a post as advocate to the Paris parlement. In 1789 the third estate of Annonay sent him to the states-general.

He helped push the assembly to declare itself the National Assembly in June 1789 and backed the taking of the Bastille. In the Convention he sat with the centre, the Marais, and voted to detain Louis XVI rather than kill him. Sent to Lyons to probe army supply frauds, he kept to the centre through the Terror. Later pages follow his part in the crises that closed the Convention and his later public career.
britannica-1911-boivin-francois-de:
François de Boivin, baron de Villars (died 1618), was a French soldier's secretary whose memoirs record the Italian wars of the 1550s. He entered the service of Marshal Brissac and went with him to Piedmont in 1550, when Brissac took command of French troops fighting Spain. He stayed in that service for years.

After the French defeat at St Quentin in 1557 he was sent to assure Henry II of Brissac's support. He also worked in the talks that led to the treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis in 1559, though he could not stop the king giving up Brissac's conquests. His Mémoires (1607) are valued as the first-hand record of an eye-witness. A revised edition appears in a great collection of French memoirs.
britannica-1911-bombelles-marc-marie-mar:
Marc Marie, marquis de Bombelles (1744–1822), was a French diplomat who ended his life as a bishop. Born at Bitsch in Lorraine, the son of the comte de Bombelles, he served in the army through the Seven Years' War. In 1765 he entered the diplomatic service.

As ambassador to Portugal in 1786 he was charged with winning that court for the Family Compact, but the queen's madness and the king's death wrecked the plan. Sent to Vienna in 1789, he lost his post in the Revolution in 1790 and worked in secret for Louis XVI. After exile in Switzerland he entered a monastery at Brünn in 1804, became bishop of Oberglogau, and in 1819 bishop of Amiens.
britannica-1911-bona-fide:
Bona fide is Latin for in good faith, and the entry explains its use as a legal term. It marks the lack of any fraud or unfair dealing in an act. The phrase is most often set before a noun, and the entry works through the three pairings a lawyer would meet.

A bona fide purchaser has bought property from its true owner, paid the price, and taken a lawful transfer, with no notice of any trust touching the land. A bona fide holder of a bill of exchange took it whole and in order, before it fell due, for value and without notice of faults in title. A bona fide traveller under the licensing acts had lodged at least 3 miles away the night before, by the nearest public road.
britannica-1911-bonne-carrere-guillaume-:
Guillaume de Bonne-Carrère (1754–1825) was a French diplomat caught up in Dumouriez's treason. Born at Muret in Languedoc, he began in the army and soon moved to foreign service under Vergennes. He was a friend of Mirabeau and of Dumouriez, and grew active as the Revolution broke.

In March 1792 Dumouriez revived for him the post of director-general of foreign affairs. He kept the old regime's diplomatic habits at the ministry until December 1792, then went to Belgium as the republic's agent. Dumouriez's treason swept him into arrest in April 1793. He printed a defence of his conduct and was freed in July 1794. Napoleon distrusted him and gave him only small missions, and after 1815 he ran a coach business between Paris and Versailles.
britannica-1911-bonneval-claude-alexandr:
Claude Alexandre, comte de Bonneval (1675–1747), later Ahmed Pasha, was a French soldier of fortune who ended in Turkish service. Born to an old Limousin family, he joined the Royal Marine Corps at thirteen and rose to command a regiment in the army. He fought in Italy and the Netherlands with dash and skill.

His insolence to the war minister brought a court-martial in 1704 and a death sentence, escaped by flight to Germany. Prince Eugene gave him an Austrian general's command against France and then Turkey. He was wounded at Peterwardein and fought with honour at Belgrade. Quarrels with Eugene ruined his Austrian rise, and the entry follows him to Constantinople, where he took Turkish service and his new name.
britannica-1911-bonnivet-guillaume-gouff:
Guillaume Gouffier, seigneur de Bonnivet (about 1488–1525), was a French soldier and royal favourite killed at Pavia. Raised alongside Francis I, he rose with the young king to great power and was made admiral of France in 1515. In the imperial election of 1519 he ran Francis's bid and spent huge sums chasing the electors' votes, in vain.

He was the sworn enemy of the constable de Bourbon and helped bring him down. Commanding in Navarre in 1521 he took Fuenterrabia, and his failure to give it back likely restarted the war. In 1523 he led the army of Italy into the Milanese, was beaten, and made a ruinous retreat in which the chevalier Bayard died. Brantôme is quoted blaming Bonnivet for urging the battle of Pavia, where he fell in 1525.
britannica-1911-bougainville-louis-antoi:
Louis Antoine de Bougainville (1729–1811) was a French soldier and navigator who sailed around the world. Born at Paris, a notary's son, he studied law, quit it, and entered the musketeers in 1753. At twenty-five he published a treatise on the integral calculus. In 1755 he served at the London embassy and joined the Royal Society.

He fought in Canada from 1756 as Montcalm's aide-de-camp, won a colonel's rank and the cross of St Louis, and served on in the Seven Years' War. After the peace he planted a Falkland Islands colony at his own cost, which France yielded to Spain on refunding him. In December 1766 he sailed with the frigate La Boudeuse and the transport L'Étoile on the voyage of discovery the entry then follows island by island.
britannica-1911-brigade:
Brigade, a word English took up in the early 17th century from French, German, Italian and Spanish forms, names an army unit led by a major-general, brigadier-general or colonel. It is built from two or more regiments of foot, horse or guns, and its exact makeup shifts with the arm it serves.

A British infantry brigade usually holds four battalions, about 4000 bayonets, with supply, transport and medical units attached. A cavalry brigade holds two or three regiments of horse. Artillery use runs smaller: a brigade of field, horse or heavy guns is a lieutenant-colonel's command of two or three batteries. Staff for a foot or horse brigade pairs the brigadier with an aide-de-camp and a brigade-major, whose duties sit between those of an adjutant and a general staff officer.
britannica-1911-brinvilliers-marie-madel:
Marie Madeleine Marguerite d'Aubray, Marquise de Brinvilliers (about 1630–1676), was a French poisoner whose case shocked Paris. Daughter of Dreux d'Aubray, civil lieutenant of Paris, she was born in the capital about 1630 and married the marquis de Brinvilliers in 1651. Witnesses of the time call her a pretty, much-courted woman with a fascinating air of childlike innocence.

In 1659 her husband presented his friend Godin de Sainte-Croix, a dashing cavalry officer of bad repute, and she became his mistress. Scandal forced her father to have Sainte-Croix seized and held a year in the Bastille, where common report says he learned poisons from the Italian Exili, a fellow prisoner. Freed, he plotted revenge on her father with her willing help. She tested the poisons he prepared, perhaps with the chemist Christopher Glaser, on the poor who sought her charity and the sick she visited.
britannica-1911-brioude:
Brioude is a town of central France, capital of an arrondissement in Haute-Loire, on the left bank of the Allier 47 miles north-west of Le Puy. It stands 1467 feet above the sea and held 4581 people in 1906. Narrow, irregular streets and many old houses and fountains survive, ringed by wide tree-lined boulevards, since the town largely escaped modern rebuilding.

One building dominates: the church of St Julian, 12th and 13th century work in the Romanesque style of Auvergne, whose choir, apse and radiating chapels show fine mosaic ornament outside. Grain trade from a fertile plain, market gardening, brewing, saw-milling, lace-making and antimony mining and founding support the town. As ancient Brinas it was once a place of weight, besieged in turn by Goths in 532, Burgundians, Saracens in 732 and Normans.
britannica-1911-briquemault-francois-de-:
Francois de Beauvais, seigneur de Briquemault (about 1502–1572), led Huguenot forces through the first French religious wars. Son of Adrien de Briquemault, he was born about 1502 and first campaigned under the count of Brissac in the Piedmont wars. Back in France in 1554 he joined Admiral Coligny, the great Protestant leader.

Charged with defending Rouen in 1562, he stood aside for Montgomery at Conde's wish and crossed to England. He settled the treaty of Hampton Court on 20 September, then returned to take Dieppe from the Catholics. In the third war he fought at Jarnac, Roche-Abeille and Montcontour, helped besiege Poitiers, relieved Vezelay and nearly took Bourges. In 1570 Coligny sent him to block the princes' army in the Rhone valley. He crossed Burgundy, joined the admiral at St Etienne in May, and shared the win at Arnay-le-Duc that June.
britannica-1911-broadside:
Broadside, sometimes called broadsheet, is a single sheet of paper printed on one side only. From the very start of printing it served for royal proclamations, papal indulgences and like public notices. England appears to have been its chief home, and there the cheap single sheet found its widest work.

Ballads were its staple, above all in the 16th century, but political agitation and personal statements of every kind also filled broadsides. The dying speeches and confessions of criminals were a grim speciality. Literature owes the form a debt too: in the later 17th century several weighty poems by Dryden, Butler and others first appeared printed on the broad side of a sheet. The entry ends with a sea sense, the firing of all guns on one side of a warship at once.
britannica-1911-brocade:
Brocade names a class of richly ornamented shuttle-woven fabrics, often made in coloured silks and worked with or without gold and silver threads. Its pattern is not printed on but woven in as an addition to the main cloth, sometimes stiffening the stuff and more often giving its face the look of low relief carving.

On the back the trick shows plainly: the loose weft threads of the brocaded parts hang in groups or are clipped away. Two pictured pieces anchor the account, Siculo-Saracenic brocades of the 11th and 12th centuries, one woven in red and olive silks with gold thread. Its Kufic inscription naming Arrahman, the Merciful, repeated over seated animals and geese set in trellis compartments. Word roots link Latin broccus to Italian and Spanish forms, and the long entry follows weave, pattern and history from there.
britannica-1911-bry-theodorus-de:
Theodorus de Bry (1528–1598), a German engraver and publisher born at Liége, is the subject of this 1911 Britannica biography. He worked first at Strassburg, then set up an engraving and publishing business at Frankfort-on-Main, and visited London in or before 1587, where he met the geographer Richard Hakluyt.

With Hakluyt's help de Bry gathered material for his finely illustrated collection of voyages, the Collectiones Peregrinationum, issued in 25 parts between 1590 and 1634. The entry also credits him with plates for Hariot's report on Virginia, for Boissard's work on Roman antiquities, and for the portrait series Icones Virorum Illustrium. He died at Frankfort on 27 March 1598, and his sons Johannes Theodorus and Johannes Israel carried the business on.
britannica-1911-capmany-y-montpalau-anto:
Antonio de Capmany y Montpalau (1742–1813) was a Spanish writer of many subjects. The entry calls him a polygraph. This short 1911 Britannica entry gives his life and books. He was born at Barcelona on 24 November 1742. He retired from the army in 1770. He later became secretary of the Royal Academy of History at Madrid. He died at Barcelona on 14 November 1813.

His chief work treats the history of his native city. It covers Barcelona's navy, trade and arts of old. It ran to four volumes, from 1779 to 1792. The entry says it still keeps much of its value. His other books treat Spanish eloquence and its history. One is a theatre of Spanish eloquence, from 1786. Another handles the philosophy of eloquence, from 1776. His critical questions of 1807 range wider still. They touch economic, political and military history together.
britannica-1911-capperonnier-claude:
Claude Capperonnier (1671–1744) was a French classical scholar. He was the son of a tanner. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career. He was born at Montdidier on 1 May 1671. He studied at Amiens and at Paris. He took orders in the Church of Rome. He gave himself almost wholly to classical studies, though. He declined a professorship at the university of Bâle.

In 1722 Capperonnier took the Greek chair at the Collège de France. He published an edition of Quintilian in 1725. At his death he left an edition of the old Latin rhetoricians. That work was published in 1756, after he died. He also supplied much material for a famous Latin thesaurus. It was Robert Estienne's Thesaurus Linguae Latinae. The entry closes with his nephew Jean Capperonnier. Jean succeeded him in the Greek chair at Paris. He edited Caesar, Anacreon, Plautus and Sophocles for readers.
britannica-1911-carbide:
A carbide is a compound of carbon with another element. This 1911 Britannica article surveys the class of compounds. The electric furnace changed the study of carbides. It let chemists prepare many metallic carbides once unknown. Some of them are now of great trade value. Calcium carbide is the outstanding case among them. The article lists the general formulas of the group.

Four main methods of preparation are classified in the text. First comes direct union of the elements at high heat. Second comes reducing oxides with carbon at high heat. Third comes reducing carbonates with magnesium and carbon together. Fourth comes the action of metals on acetylene. The metallic carbides are crystalline solids, as a rule. Most of them break down in water. They yield a metallic hydrate and a hydrocarbon gas. Calcium carbide gives acetylene gas in that reaction. That gas is the source of its industrial importance.
britannica-1911-carbon-bisulphide:
Carbon bisulphide is a chemical liquid, with formula CS2. This 1911 Britannica article gives its making and cleaning. W. A. Lampadius first discovered it in 1796. He made it by heating charcoal with pyrites. A handier method passes sulphur vapour over red-hot charcoal. The gases then flow through towers of oiled plates. The oil catches any bisulphide vapour in the stream.

A second tower holds lime for the gas. The lime absorbs the sulphuretted hydrogen present. The crude product is very impure at this stage. It also carries an offensive smell. Lime water sprayed through it cleans it well. The washing goes on until the escaping water runs clear. The article follows the pure liquid's properties from there. Its uses and its dangers get their share of the text.
britannica-1911-carronade:
Carronade is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a short naval gun invented by General Robert Melville (1728–1809). He designed the piece in 1759 and called it the “smasher,” applying an old principle of gun construction. The British navy did not adopt it until 1779. By then it took its name from the Carron works in Stirlingshire, Scotland, where Mr Gascoigne first cast it.

The gun had a powder chamber like the earliest cannon and resembled a mortar. It was short and light, with a limited range, but it proved destructive at close quarters. Ships added carronades on top of their long guns, so a 38-gun frigate carrying ten carronades actually bore 48 pieces. Official ratings never changed to match, which made them poor guides to a ship's real strength. The entry notes that French and American navies later took up the weapon too.
britannica-1911-carvajal-luisa-de:
Luisa de Carvajal (1568–1614) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Spanish missionary in England. She was born at Jaraicejo in Estremadura. Her father headed an old and wealthy family. Her mother came from the great house of Mendoza. Both parents died of fever in 1572. They had caught it while visiting the poor. Luisa passed to a grand aunt, then to her uncle, the count of Almazan.

The count's religious zeal ran to harsh asceticism. Luisa matched it. She sent her own dinner to the poor. She wore a chain next to her skin. At seventeen she submitted to servants set over her. At the count's order they scourged and trampled her. Yet when she came of age she refused to enter a religious house. She chose mission work on her own terms instead. That path took her to England.
britannica-1911-centipede:
Centipede is a long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the typical member of the Chilopoda, a class of arthropods. Centipedes were once grouped with the millipedes and two smaller groups in the class Myriapoda. That grouping is now abandoned. The likeness between centipedes and millipedes is mostly on the surface. Both have long, worm like bodies made of many similar segments. Neither divides those segments into functional series, as insects do.

The entry gives the turning point in classification. Until 1893 no one doubted the old grouping. In that year Pocock and Kingsley, working apart, showed that the two groups differ from each other as much as either differs from the insects. They should rank as separate classes. Pocock tied the centipedes to the insects in one great group. The split rests on where the generative openings sit on the body.
britannica-1911-chastelard-pierre-de-boc:
Pierre de Bocsozel de Chastelard (1540–1563) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French poet from Dauphiné, of the house of Bayard. His name is bound up with Mary, queen of Scots. As a page he passed from the Constable Montmorency's service to Marshal Damville's. He escorted Mary to Scotland in 1561. He returned to Scotland soon after, carrying letters for her and poems by Ronsard, his master in song.

Chastelard fell in love with the queen. Verse passed between them, and she showed him open favour. He hid himself under her bed and was found by her maids of honour. Mary pardoned him, and the old terms resumed. He did it again, was seized, and was hanged the next morning. On the way to the scaffold he read Ronsard's Hymne de la mort. The entry warns that its source, Brantôme, is notoriously untrustworthy.
britannica-1911-chaulieu-guillaume-amfry:
Guillaume Amfrye de Chaulieu (1639–1720) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French poet and wit born at Fontenay in Normandy. His father was a maître des comptes at Rouen and sent him to the Collège de Navarre. His early wit won him the favour of the duke of Vendôme. The duke procured him the abbey of Aumale and other benefices.

Chaulieu became the constant companion of the duke and his brother at the Temple in Paris. Their circle there was gay and reckless. He travelled to Poland in the suite of the marquis de Béthune, hoping for a court career under John Sobieski. He returned without advancement. Saint-Simon accused him of helping the grand prior rob the duke, a charge Sainte-Beuve later questioned. His best known poems are “Fontenay” and “La Retraite.” He died in June 1720.
britannica-1911-chazelles-jean-mathieu-d:
Jean Mathieu de Chazelles (1657–1710) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French hydrographer born at Lyons. In 1685 he became professor of hydrography at Marseilles. In that post he carried out various coast surveys. In 1693 he was engaged to publish a second volume of the Neptune français. The volume was to cover the hydrography of the Mediterranean.

For that work Chazelles visited the Levant and Egypt. In Egypt he measured the pyramids. He found that the angles of the largest pyramid's sides pointed to the four cardinal points. From that he concluded that the position must have been intended. He also concluded that the earth's poles and meridians had not shifted since the pyramids were built. He was made a member of the Academy in 1695. He died in Paris in January 1710.
britannica-1911-chenier-andre-de:
André de Chénier (1762–1794) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French poet born at Constantinople. His father, a cloth merchant from Languedoc, held a post equal to French consul there. His mother was Greek. When André was three the family returned to France. His father later served as consul general in Morocco, while the family stayed in France.

The boy ran wild for some years with an aunt at Carcassonne. He then shone at the Collège de Navarre in Paris as a verse translator from the classics. In 1783 he took a cadetship at Strassburg, but the glamour of army life soon faded. He returned to Paris within the year. His mother's salon drew a cultivated circle, among them Lavoisier and the painter David. A visit to Rome in 1784 confirmed his love of the antique.
britannica-1911-chenier-marie-joseph-bla:
Marie Joseph Blaise de Chénier (1764–1811) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French poet and dramatist, the younger brother of André de Chénier. He was born at Constantinople and educated at the Collège de Navarre in Paris. He entered the army at seventeen and left it two years later. At nineteen he produced two plays, both failures. His Charles IX was then held back by the censor for nearly two years.

Chénier attacked the censorship in three pamphlets, and the storm raised interest in the play. Produced in November 1789, Charles IX was an immense success, helped by Talma's acting. Desmoulins said it had done more for the Revolution than the days of October. Henri VIII, in 1791, is generally taken as his masterpiece. His Caius Gracchus of 1792 was yet more revolutionary. It was banned in 1793 for a line against bloodshed.
britannica-1911-cienfuegos-nicasio-alvar:
Cienfuegos, Nicasio Álvarez de (1764–1809) was a Spanish poet and publicist, born at Madrid on 14 December 1764. He studied with distinction at Salamanca, where he met the poet Meléndez Valdés, and his poems, published in 1778, drew attention at once. He edited the Gaceta and the Mercurio in turn. An article against Napoleon brought him a death sentence, commuted on his friends' petition to deportation to France.

He died at Orthez early in the following year, closing a short career shaped by that clash. His verses follow the model of Meléndez Valdés, with sound technique and passion, the entry says. False sentiment and the thin philosophy of the age mar them, and archaisms and gallicisms drew blame. Four tragedies on the French classic model and one comedy are judged deservedly forgotten.
britannica-1911-clairault-alexis-claude:
Clairault, Alexis Claude (1713–1765) was a French mathematician, born at Paris on 7 or 13 May 1713, where his father taught mathematics. Under his father's tuition he advanced so fast that at thirteen he read the French Academy an account of four curves he had discovered. At sixteen he finished a treatise on curves of double curvature, printed in 1731. Publication won him admission to the Academy of Sciences below the legal age.

In 1736 he joined Maupertuis on the Lapland expedition to measure a degree of the meridian, and his Théorie de la figure de la terre followed in 1743. Clairault's theorem in that work links gravity on a rotating ellipsoid with compression and centrifugal force at the equator. He found an approximate solution of the three bodies problem, won a St Petersburg prize for his theory of the moon in 1750, and calculated the perihelion of Halley's comet in 1759.
britannica-1911-clermont-tonnerre-stanis:
Clermont-Tonnerre, Stanislas Marie Adelaide, Comte de (1757–1792) was a French politician, born at Pont-à-Mousson on 10 October 1757. At the Revolution's beginning he was a colonel with a reputation as a freemason and a Liberal. Elected to the states-general of 1789 by the noblesse of Paris, he spoke for the minority of Liberal nobles who joined the Third Estate on 25 June. He wished to model France's new constitution on that of England.

Elected president of the Constituent Assembly on 17 August 1789, he later joined the moderate royalist monarchiens under Malouet. His speech for an absolute royal veto drew the wrath of advanced politicians, yet he kept advocating moderate liberal policy. Rights for Jews and Protestants and wider trial by jury were among his causes. He helped found the Club des Impartiaux in 1790, and a mob murdered him during the rising of 9 and 10 August 1792.
britannica-1911-clyde:
Clyde, in Welsh Clwyd, is the principal river of Lanarkshire, Scotland, and also the name of the estuary forming the largest and finest firth on the west coast. Daer Water and Potrail Water, rising in hilly country on the Lanarkshire and Dumfriesshire borders, unite south of Elvanfoot to form the river. Many mountain burns also feed those headstreams. An old rhyme claiming that Annan, Tweed and Clyde rise from one hillside is not true, the entry says.

From the junction the river runs mainly north, winding around Tinto Hill and by Carstairs, then north-west from above Lanark. It is generally held to end as a river at Dumbarton, where it merges in the Firth. Tributaries named include the Medwin, the Mouse at Lanark and the South Calder. Course, tributaries, falls and the firth fill out the full survey that follows in the article.
britannica-1911-cockade:
A cockade is a knot of ribbons or a rosette worn as a badge. It now forms part of the dress of servants in livery. The word comes from the French cocarde, linked to the cock's comb. At first the cockade was the button and loop that held up the side of a slouch hat.

Party badges grew from that plain loop of cloth. The Stuarts used a white rose, and the white cockade lived on in Jacobite song. William III used yellow. The House of Hanover brought in black, still worn by royal coachmen and grooms in England. The entry traces cockades on French and English headgear as well. In time the badge shrank to a mark of service dress.
britannica-1911-conde:
Condé is the name of some twenty villages in France and of two towns of real weight. Condé-en-Brie was in the middle ages the seat of a small principality. Condé-sur-Aisne passed in 870 from Charles the Bald to a Rouen abbey. Condé-sur-Marne keeps a parish church with a fine Romanesque tower. The entry gives each place its own short past.

The first town is Condé-sur-l'Escaut in the department of Nord. It stands where the Scheldt and Condé-Mons canals meet. Its commune held 5,310 people in 1906. Coal and cattle drive its trade. Brewing, rope-making and boat-building fill its works. Great age marks the place as well. The second town lies in Normandy, with a castle held by the English from 1417 to 1449. Ruins of that castle still stand.
britannica-1911-condorcet-marie-jean-ant:
Marie Jean Antoine Nicolas Caritat, marquis de Condorcet (1743–1794), was a French mathematician, philosopher and revolutionary. He was born at Ribemont in Picardy on 17 September 1743. His family took their title from Condorcet, near Nyons in Dauphiné. His father died while he was very young. His devout mother had him schooled by Jesuits at Reims and at the College of Navarre in Paris.

Maths brought his first fame. At sixteen his work in analysis won praise from D'Alembert and Clairaut. At twenty-two he wrote a treatise on the integral calculus that won warm approval. Yet his many-sided mind could not stay in one field. Philosophy and letters drew him as well. Social work, the entry says, was dearer to him than any branch of thought alone. The long entry follows that wide life through the Revolution years.
britannica-1911-couvade:
Couvade is a custom found among several peoples in far parts of the world. Its name means, in plain terms, a brooding, from a French verb for hatching. The custom binds the father at the birth of his child. He takes to his bed at that time, and at times before it. He fasts or shuns set foods while he lies there. Care of the kind shown to women in childbed comes to him instead.

Old writers vouch for the custom in classical times. Apollonius Rhodius names it, and Diodorus places it among the Corsicans. Strabo found it among the Spanish Basques. Men said the Basques and Gascons kept it still, though fresh inquiry casts doubt on that claim. Marco Polo found it in Chinese Turkestan. Travellers since have found it in China, India, Borneo, Siam, Africa and the Americas. Traces of it linger in parts of Europe as well.
britannica-1911-crayer-gaspard-de:
Gaspard de Crayer (1582–1669) was a Flemish painter born at Antwerp who learned painting from Raphael Coxcie. He joined the guild of St Luke at Brussels in 1607 and lived in that city until after 1660. He then settled at Ghent, where he died. Albert and Isabella, who governed the Netherlands, treated him well, and the cardinal-infant Ferdinand made him a court painter.

Crayer ranks among the most productive yet careful painters of the later Flemish school. The entry places him second to Rubens in vigour and below Vandyck in refinement, yet near both in most skills of painting. His works fill churches and museums in Brussels and Ghent, and many country chapels hold his canvases. Named works include the Miraculous Draught of Fishes at Brussels and the Judgment of Solomon at Ghent. Panels for a triumphal arch show his skill in large decorative work.
britannica-1911-crebillon-prosper-jolyot:
The hosted text opens partway through its account, with a closing judgment on the drama of Prosper Jolyot de Crébillon. It calls his plays forceful but marred by scenes of unnatural horror and by careless verse, with fine passages here and there. It also notes a hostile Éloge of 1762, widely ascribed to Voltaire, who denied writing it. Editions of his works and a study by Maurice Dutrait are then listed.

Most of the hosted text covers his son, Claude Prosper Jolyot Crébillon (1707–1777), a French novelist born in Paris. His satire L'Écumoire of 1734 brought disgrace, prison, and five years of exile. He later helped found the Caveau dining society and served as a censor from 1759. His best known novels include Les Amours de Zéokinizul and Le Sopha, both from 1740. He died in Paris on 12 April 1777.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adelaide:
Adelaide is the archdiocese centred on South Australia's capital city. It covers all South Australia south of Victoria and Burra counties to Northwest Bend. The River Murray then forms the boundary to New South Wales. Flinders, Musgrave, and Jervois counties form its western portion, with adjacent islands. Its area is 40,320 square miles.

A chartered company founded South Australia in 1836 as a free, non-convict, Protestant colony. Papists and pagans were meant to be excluded, yet a few Catholics came among the first immigrants. Dr. Ullathorne visited Adelaide in June 1840. Governor Gawler refused the government school for Mass, so a generous Protestant lent a store where the first Mass drew about fifty. Adelaide became a see in 1843, with Francis Murphy its first bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-of-sta:
Albert of Stade chronicled the thirteenth century, having been born in the late 1100s. In 1232 he took charge as abbot of Stade's Benedictine house near Hamburg. In 1236 he tried to replace his abbey's Benedictine rule with the Cistercian rule, and resigned when he failed. In 1240 he joined the Franciscans and began his chronicle the same year.

His chronicle runs from the creation of the world down to 1256, with possible continuations to 1265. Its early parts draw on Bede's book on the six ages of the world and Ekkehard's chronicle. The entry notes that Albert grows fuller and more reliable as he nears his own times. The first complete edition appeared at Helmstadt in 1587, and he is also credited with Troilus, a Latin poem on Troy running to 5,320 lines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-side:
The altar side is the part facing the congregation, as opposed to the side where the priest formerly stood facing the people. Ceremonials often mention the altar's right and left sides. Before 1488, right meant the epistle side and left the gospel side.

In that year Augustine Patrizi, Bishop of Pienza, issued a ceremonial that named the epistle side left and the gospel side right. The denomination came from the cross's facing alone, not the priest's or the laity's. St. Pius V accepted the change and put it into the rubrics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-averbode:
Averbode is a Premonstratensian abbey in the circary of Brabant, near Diest in the Archdiocese of Malines. Count Arnold of Losen founded it about 1132, and it ran without break until the general suppression of Belgian monasteries in 1796. The abbey was restored in 1834. At present it counts 82 priests, 20 clerics and novices, and 36 lay brothers.

Of those members, 27 priests and 21 lay brothers labor among the Indians in Brazil. At Leo XIII's request they set up a missionary monastery at Pirapora in the Diocese of Sao Paulo in 1896. They added a college at Jaguarao in the Diocese of Sao Pedro do Rio Grande do Sul in 1901. More recently two priests and three lay brothers from Averbode opened a mission house at Veile in Denmark. The entry cites Hugo's annals of the order and its general catalogue for the house's story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bede:
Bede is the old English word for a prayer, from Anglo-Saxon bed, though gebed was the commoner form. In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, little perforated globes of bone, wood, or amber, strung to count prayers, took the name bedes. Our modern bead, for small glass or coral globes, derives from nothing else. In middle English, bedes meant both prayer and rosary, as Shakespeare's plays and Chaucer's Prioress show.

The gauds were larger beads dividing the decades, and a pair of beads still means the five-decade chaplet, not the full rosary. To bid beads first meant simply to say prayers, though bidding the beads later attached to certain public devotions. Bede-roll meant the roll of those to be prayed for, kept by early English guilds for departed members. The word survives provincially and in Welsh place-names like Bettws y Coed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bull-of-the-c:
The Bull of the Crusade granted indulgences to fighters in wars against the infidels, above all in Spain's reconquest. Such grants reached back to the eleventh century, when the Spanish Mark's faithful earned them by building churches or giving alms. The first Spanish crusade bulls came from Urban II in 1089 for Barcelona's counts at Tarragona's reconquest and from Gelasius II in 1118 for Alfonso I of Aragon at Saragossa.

Clement IV extended a bull to all Spain in 1265 for the Murcia expedition, and grants multiplied under the Catholic kings in 1478 through 1505 and beyond. Alms first funded war alone, then church building and pious works, and at times state expenses, despite Cortes protests in 1523 and 1592 and Philip III's rules. After 1847 the funds endowed churches and clergy by law in 1849 and the Concordat of 1851. The faithful, confessed and communicated, gained a plenary indulgence, double absolution from reserved sins, and commutation of hard vows.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-certitude:
Certitude names a state of mind on the one hand and a quality of a proposition on the other, whether the phrase is I am certain or It is certain. Philosophy marks the distinction as subjective certitude and objective certitude. Newman reserves certitude for the state of mind and uses certainty for the condition of a proposition's evidence.
