Certitude is correlative to truth, since truth is the intellect's object. We commonly call a proposition certain when its truth is so evident as rightly to produce certitude. Certitude stands against ignorance, doubt, and opinion, the last meaning in the strict sense the holding of a proposition as probable. Certitude itself is assent to a proposition's truth that excludes all real doubt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-judde:
Claude Judde, a French preacher and spiritual father, was born at Rouen about 20 December 1661 and died at Paris on 11 March 1735. He joined the Society of Jesus on 18 September 1677, taking final vows on 2 February 1695. At first he preached with success in the provinces and the capital, and his oratorical gifts were judged equal to Bourdaloue's. Bourdaloue even wished him as successor and spoke of bequeathing his papers.

Judde's superiors instead asked him to give up pulpit success for training his brethren in religious virtues. From 1704 to 1721 he instructed the third probation at Rouen and served as rector of the Paris novitiate. Hearers of his retreats and exhortations, charmed by solid eloquence at once vigorous and pathetic, preserved his words in writing. He published nothing himself, but after his death collections appeared from transcripts. They include a spiritual retreat of 1746, Christian reflections of 1748, exhortations of 1772, and complete spiritual works of 1781 to 1782.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claudio-monte:
Claudio Monteverde, a distinguished musician, was born at Cremona in May 1567 and died at Venice on 29 November 1643. He studied under Ingegneri and published a book of canzonets at sixteen, followed by four volumes of madrigals. One madrigal of 1592 already shows his inventive turn, with suspensions of the dominant seventh and suspended ninths. He became the Duke of Mantua's Maestro di Cappella in 1602 and at Venice in 1613. His Venice salary rose to five hundred ducats in 1616.

Until his death he produced choral works, operas, cantatas, and ballets, most now untraced. The score of Orfeo, printed in 1609, survives and shows a musician breaking from the older school to create his own. His novelties include new instrumental effects and combinations, an instrumental tremolo in a festival interlude, and trombones accompanying a Mass's Gloria and Credo in 1631. His fame rests on unprepared discords, improved recitative, and a revolution in orchestration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-colonnade:
Thomas Poole's entry defines a colonnade as a set of columns arranged in one or more rows, set in symmetry. A single row makes it monostyle, while many rows make it polystyle. When it rings a building or court, it is called a peristyle. When it juts past the building line, it is a portico. Sometimes it bears a building. Sometimes it bears only a roof. The terms sort a common sight of classical building into clear kinds.

For church building, the most famous example stands at Saint Peter's in Rome. Bernini raised it in 1665 to 1667, with 284 columns. Above its balustrades stand 162 statues of saints. Poole points readers to the Bernini entry for more. Short as it is, the entry gives a builder or visitor the words to name each form of columned walk.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Sister St. Beatrice's entry follows the Sisters of Misericorde, a women's congregation founded on 16 January 1848 to give spiritual and corporal help to poor mothers and unfortunate girls. Foundress Rosalie Jette, in religion Mother Mary of the Nativity, declined the superior's office, so Sister Saint Jane de Chantal held it. Pius IX approved the institute on 7 June 1867. Constitutions revised under Rome's latest rules won Pius X's approbation on 21 March 1905.

A superior general governs, assisted by four councillors, a secretary, and a bursar, all resident at Montreal's mother-house in Canada. Branch houses answer to general administration, each under a local superior, two assistants forming her council, and a bursar for temporal matters controlled by that council. Present numbers count 189 professed sisters, 23 novices, and 10 candidates. American houses include Milwaukee, Oak Park in Illinois founded in 1905 with fifteen sisters and 712 patients, and a Wisconsin house from 1900 serving 450 patients and children yearly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cornelius-cor:
John Peter Van Kasteren's entry treats Cornelius Cornelii a Lapide, Cornelis Cornelissen van den Steen, Flemish Jesuit and exegete. Born at Bocholt in Flemish Limburg in 1567, he died at Rome in 1637. He studied humanities and philosophy at Maestricht and Cologne, theology first for half a year at Douai, then for four years at Louvain. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1592, and, after two years' noviciate and another theology year, was ordained priest in 1595.

After teaching philosophy for half a year, he became Louvain's professor of Scripture in 1596, and of Hebrew the next year. In 1616 Rome called him in the same capacity, where on 3 November he assumed an office he filled with renown for years. His later years seem devoted to finishing his commentaries. Cornelius a Lapide wrote ample commentaries on all Catholic Canon books except Job and the Psalms. Their numerous editions show how highly Catholics estimate the works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-ag:
The Council of Agde met in 506 at Agde in Languedoc, under St Caesarius of Arles, with thirty-five bishops in attendance. Its forty-seven genuine canons govern church discipline in southern France at the moment the Graeco-Roman order gave way to barbarian conquerors. They also matter for the study of certain early church institutions.

One canon, the seventh, bars clergy from selling or alienating church property that supports them, an early hint of the later benefice system. Taken together, the canons open a window on clergy and laity alike, and on a society changing masters while its church rules stayed in force.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-deus-in-adjut:
A liturgical entry on Deus in adjutorium meum intende, the first verse of Psalm 69, with its answer asking the Lord to hasten to help. These words open each Hour in Roman, monastic, and Ambrosian use, except in the last three days of Holy Week and the Office of the Dead. All present sign themselves with the cross as the words are said or sung.

Tradition credits Saint Benedict with bringing the custom into monastic prayer and Saint Gregory the First with spreading it to Roman churches, though Cassian reports monks using it from the earliest times. Placed first, the plea begs God's aid against wandering thoughts in prayer. Orderings differ by rite and Hour, and in Prime the verse returns three times, while monks once sang it threefold to bind prayer to labour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epistle-of-sa:
The Epistle of Saint Jude is treated here under five heads for its author and authenticity, then its analysis, occasion, readers, and date and place. The author calls himself Jude, servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James. That James is the Bishop of Jerusalem, called by Paul the brother of the Lord and author of the Epistle of James.

Most Catholic commentators identify Jude with Judas Jacobi of Luke and Acts, also called Thaddeus. His brother James was better known than he in the early Church. If that identification holds, Jude ranked among the Twelve Apostles, an opinion the entry calls most highly probable. Beyond the New Testament we learn little more of Jude. The brethren of the Lord, Jude among them, were known to Galatians and Corinthians, and several of them were married.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eustache-merc:
Eustache Mercade was a French dramatic poet of the fifteenth century whose dates of birth and death are unknown. A document found only recently shows he was removed from that office in 1427 but restored in 1437. The restoration came by a ruling of the Châtelet court, confirmed by Paris's Parliament on 2 May 1439. Martin Franc, writing in the middle of the century, ranked him among the most famous rhetoricians, or skilled verse-makers, of the day.

Mercade's name survives on a great Mystery play, The Life, the Passion, and the Vengeance of Jesus Christ, kept in the library of Arras. Only the last part, the Vengeance, is judged to be his own work. It holds 312 characters, of whom 112 have speaking parts, a scale that shows the size of late medieval religious drama.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-facade:
Facade means the front of any building. In church building it most often means the west front. For ritual reasons, the architect had to make the nave's end wall the grand façade. Early Christian façades copied old Roman basilicas, using Roman methods and columns taken from pagan buildings.

Their upper parts were very plain, with two types ruling: the central gable tracing the structure behind, and the screen façade jutting out for shelter. Great churches hid the whole surface in mosaic from summit to porch. Saint John Lateran, Saint Peter, Saint Paul, and Saint Mary Major blazed with color above the porch. Byzantine fronts stayed plain, entered through a forecourt with a fountain for washing, and a narthex led by three doors into church. Lombard façades fared worst, with false fronts, though Saint Ambrose at Milan stands as their best.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fortitude:
Fortitude is the virtue of steady courage, from the Latin virtus, manliness, and the Greek andreia. In early cultures it meant little more than the brave strength that defends life and kin, but Plato, Aristotle, and St. Thomas Aquinas refined it into something guided by reason. Thomas ranks it third among the cardinal virtues, after prudence and justice. He insists that raw animal spirit must be taken up and steered by the rational soul before it counts as virtue.

The entry works through the old definitions, the difference between true courage and mere boldness found even in children and animals. It also covers the role of fear and daring in moral life. It also treats the bodily side: health, freshness of spirit, and mastery over terror, as when a soldier outgrows his first fear of cannon fire. Moral and physical courage, it argues, must be trained together.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-bour:
Francois Bourgade, born at Gaujan in the Gers on 7 July 1806 and dead at Paris on 21 May 1866. He was a French missionary and philosopher who worked among Muslims. He studied theology at Auch seminary and was ordained in 1832. After his request for African missions was granted in 1838, he went to Algeria, served in hospitals, then crossed to Tunis, where he founded a hospital and schools.

He took charge of the chapel Louis Philippe had built where St. Louis died, and received decorations including the Legion of Honour. His writings aimed to spread Christian knowledge among Muslims. They include Soirees de Carthage in 1847, La clef du Coran in 1852, Passage du Coran a l'Evangile in 1855. A philological work on the golden fleece of the Phoenician language and a letter refuting Renan's Life of Jesus in 1864 complete the list. The entry presents a missionary who argued through language, history, and charity rather than force.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frederic-fran:
Xavier de Mérode, a Belgian soldier turned priest, ended his public life as minister of war to Pius IX. Born at Brussels in 1820 to a statesman's family, he served with French forces in Algeria. He won the Legion of Honour there. In 1847 he quit the army for the priesthood and was ordained at Rome two years later. The entry follows a restless aristocrat who kept trading one career for another.

At Rome he ran the papal prisons with reforms that even critics praised. Then in 1860 he talked Pius IX into raising a papal army against Piedmont, with Lamoricière in command. Defeat at Castelfidardo and Ancona owed more to treachery and poor supplies than to the chiefs, the entry argues. Mérode spent his later years on public works, including building at his own cost.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guillaume-bud:
Paris Hellenist Guillaume Budé, born in 1467, turned from a careless student into France's leading Greek scholar and the founder of its national library. After Greek lessons from Hermonymus and advice from Lascaris, he mastered Greek, philosophy, theology, law, and medicine, served Louis XII as secretary, and carried embassies to Rome.

At his urging Francis I planned a college for Greek, Hebrew, and Latin, later the Collège de France. He refused the Sorbonne's call to ban printing in 1533 and built the Fontainebleau library that grew into the Bibliothèque Nationale. His commentaries on Greek, his notes applying philology to Roman law, and his treatise on Roman coins reshaped French learning before his death in 1540.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-homicide:
Homicide, from Latin words for man and slaying, means, generally, one human being's killing of another. In practice it means the unjust taking of human life by a person other than the victim, acting privately. Suicide and lawful execution therefore fall outside this article's scope.

Direct killing of an innocent person ranks among the gravest sins. It happens directly when death is sought as an end or chosen as a means. Its malice lies first in violating God's supreme ownership of human life, and second in outraging the cherished human right to life. A person counts as innocent until some responsible act has brought hurt comparable to loss of life. Indirect homicide, where death forms no part of the agent's plan, is treated separately.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-infanticide:
Killing a newborn or very young child is the crime traced here across law and custom. French law narrowed the word to the murder of a newborn, while English use stretched from conception to the age of two or three. Outside Hebrew and Christian law, the entry says, parents who killed very young children were almost always allowed to do so by law or left unpunished in practice.

Money drove the practice more than anything else, the entry argues. Girl infants suffered most where daughters were seen as costly and unproductive, above all where large dowries were due with them. Poetic and religious tales were sometimes cited in the East to excuse the custom, but the economic root stayed clear. In India the practice ran far into modern times before law and mission work pressed against it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacob-balde:
German poet Jacob Balde was born at Ensisheim in Upper Alsace on 4 January 1604. He died at Neuburg on 9 August 1668. He studied classics and rhetoric at his town's Jesuit college. He studied philosophy and law at Ingolstadt university. On 1 July 1624 he entered the Society of Jesus. He taught classics and rhetoric at Munich and Innsbruck.

In his spare hours he wrote the Latin mock-heroic Batrachomyomachia, or Battle of Frogs and Mice. After theology studies at Ingolstadt, he was ordained priest in 1633. He became professor of eloquence at the university. Later he moved to Munich to tutor Duke Albert's sons. He then served as court preacher to Elector Maximilian. Failing health sent him to Neuburg in 1654. The entry follows a Jesuit wit turned court preacher.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-michel-d:
Jean-Michel d'Astorg Aubarède, born in 1639 and dead in 1692, he served as canon regular and vicar capitular of Pamiers. He studied at Toulouse, entered Pamiers seminary, and joined the canons who formed its cathedral chapter. On Bishop Caulet's death the chapter chose him administrator.

Aubarède carried on Caulet's resistance to royal claims over the régale, the king's right to church revenues and appointments during a vacancy. He refused royal nominees to benefices and excommunicated canons the king named when they tried to act. Arrested by royal order, he spent six years imprisoned at Caen, where he died, a witness to church freedom in an age of royal sway.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joachim-barra:
Joachim Barrande, a French palaeontologist born in 1799 and dead near Vienna in 1883. He studied at the École Polytechnique and was chosen by Charles X to tutor his grandson, the duke of Bordeaux. When the king abdicated in 1830 Barrande followed the family to England, Scotland, and Prague, staying the duke's friend and estate manager for life.

Barrande's passion became Bohemia's fossils, a field then barely touched. Walking surveys of the Silurian district in the 1840s, some 140 square miles, opened forty-three years of quarrying, naming, and picturing specimens. His Silurian System of Central Bohemia, begun in 1852, stands near unrivalled in fossil literature for scale and care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-gage-rok:
John Gage Rokewode was an English antiquary whose edition of Jocelin de Brakelond fed Carlyle's Past and Present. Born in 1786, fourth son of Sir Thomas Gage of Hengrave, he took the name Rokewode in 1838 on succeeding to the estates. Educated at Stonyhurst and called to the bar after studying under Charles Butler, he never practiced, preferring antiquarian pursuits.

Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries from 1818 and its director from 1829 to 1842, he published histories of Hengrave in 1822 and of Suffolk in 1838. His Camden Society edition of Jocelin's chronicle in 1840 supplied Carlyle with much material. His papers in Archaeologia included descriptions of the benedictionals of St. Aethelwold and Robert of Jumieges, and he contributed to Catholic journals before dying suddenly while out shooting in 1842.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-justin-timoth:
Justin Timotheus Balthasar von Linde was a Hessian jurist and statesman, from lecture hall to German Diet. Born at Brilon in 1797, he lost his father at three; his widowed mother raised four children in wartime. He studied law at Münster, Göttingen, and Bonn, took his doctorate in 1820, and drew large numbers lecturing at Giessen. Darmstadt called him in 1829 as ministerial counsel; he later directed its Board of Education.

He became Giessen's Chancellor in 1833, a privy councillor in 1836, and a nobleman in 1839, retiring on a pension in 1847. He sat in the Frankfurt Parliament of 1848 and Erfurt's of 1850, then served Liechtenstein as ambassador to the German Diet until its dissolution in 1866. A particularist and zealous defender of Church rights, he founded Giessen's Catholic theological faculty and helped raise a church. The wreck of his political ideals in 1866 broke his cheerfulness and his capacity for work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mary-francis-:
Mary Francis Xavier Warde was born at Belbrook House, Mountrath, Queen's County, Ireland, in 1810 and died at Manchester, New Hampshire, in 1884. Motherless in infancy, she was raised by a maternal great-aunt in Fenelon's method. Gay by nature and drawn to fashionable frivolity, scruples led her to her director, who set her helping the Sisters of Mercy's foundress teach homeless children.

In 1837 she became superior of Carlow convent, built under her eye and the congregation's first house outside Dublin. She founded Naas in 1839 and Wexford in 1840, whose orphan asylum soon joined it, and Sligo with its flourishing teacher training school. In 1843 Pittsburgh's Bishop O'Connor sought a Carlow foundation, opening her American work. From 1852 she opened Hartford and New Haven houses with free schools, then academies, Newport in 1854, Rochester in 1857, and Manchester in 1858.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mende:
Mende, a French diocese covering the department of Lozere, was suffragan of Bourges under the old regime. The Concordat of 1801 restored it as a suffragan of Lyons, joined to Ardeche, and in 1822 it lost that department to the new Diocese of Viviers and became suffragan of Albi. Late legends say St. Martial passed through the Gabali country, of which Mende is capital, and named his disciple St. Severian its first bishop about the first century's start.

The first bishop known to history is St. Privatus, who by Gregory of Tours's account died in a grotto of Mount Mimmat, a victim of ill treatment during the Alamanni invasion under King Chrocus. Gregory sets the event about 260, Fredegarius in 407, and Duchesne near Constantine's reign. An organized church certainly stood in Gabali country by 314, since it sent representatives to Arles that year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paschal-tide:
Paschal Tide covers the fifty days from Easter Sunday to Pentecost, called by older liturgists the Paschal Fifty or Fifty of Joy. Easter's octave, part and crown of the solemnity, has its own office. In liturgical books Paschal Tide runs from First Vespers of Low Sunday to before First Vespers of Trinity Sunday, with each Sunday bearing its own title.

Low Sunday, or Sunday in White, leads, and the second Sunday, from its Gospel, is Good Shepherd Sunday, or from its introit, Misericordias Domini. Local feasts crowd the season. Armenians honour the faithful departed on Easter Sunday. Greeks keep Our Lady the Living Fountain on Easter Friday. Russians carry Easter eggs to graves on Tuesday of Low week. Portuguese and Brazilian dioceses feast Mary's joys at her Son's rising.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-passiontide:
Passiontide is the two weeks from Passion Sunday to Easter, the last being Holy Week and the first the Latins' Week of the Passion and the Greeks' Week of the Palms. Eastern desert monks returned to their monasteries in this season. Roman rubrics order crosses, statues, and pictures of Our Lord and saints veiled in violet, opaque and unadorned, before Vespers of the Saturday before Passion Sunday.

Crosses stay veiled until the chief crucifix is unveiled on Good Friday, while statues and pictures keep veils until the Gloria of Holy Saturday, whatever feasts fall between. One tolerance lets Saint Joseph's statue outside the sanctuary stay bare in March. In Masses of the season the Judica psalm drops, Gloria Patri leaves Asperges, introit, and Lavabo, only two orations are said, and the Preface is of the Holy Cross.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-van-de-:
Peter van de Velde, better known as Pedro Campaña, was a Brussels painter who belongs to the Spanish school. Born in 1503 as Pieter de Kempeneer, he spent his early years in Italy studying Raphael and calling himself his pupil. In 1530 he painted triumphal scenery for Charles V's coronation, then left for Spain on Cardinal Grimani's advice, returning to Brussels only about 1563.

With Luis de Vargas and the sculptor Torrigiano he founded a Seville painting school between 1537 and 1562, which grew into the city's academy and taught Morales. His masterpiece, the Descent from the Cross of 1548 for Santa Cruz, now hangs in Seville Cathedral, with his Purification and Resurrection beside it. Other churches across Seville hold his work. Murillo asked to be buried near Campaña's picture. He died at Brussels in 1580.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-heude:
Pierre Heude was a French Jesuit priest who worked in China as a missionary and a student of animal life. He was born at Fougères in 1836. He joined the Jesuits in 1856 and was ordained in 1867. He reached China the next year and stayed there until his death at Zi-ka-wei near Shanghai in 1902.

He began with plants, then turned to animals. Between 1868 and 1881 he travelled by river through central and eastern China to study freshwater shellfish. Later he founded a natural history museum at Zi-ka-wei. His later journeys across Southeast Asia fed long studies of mammals, above all how teeth and bones mark out species and families.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pride:
Pride is the over love of one's own worth. It is commonly counted among the seven capital sins. St Thomas, following St Gregory, names it the queen of all vices, setting vainglory in its place among the deadly sins. In taking it so high, he reads it in its fullest sense. It is the mind's frame in which a man, through love of his own worth, seeks to slip from subjection to Almighty God and scorns superiors' commands. 

 By it the creature refuses to stay in his rightful orbit. He turns his back on God, not from weakness or ignorance, but solely from self praise, refusing to submit.  A milder pride pushes a man to make too much of himself with no good warrant, yet with no wish to cast off the Creator's rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raymond-of-sa:
Raymond of Sabunde was born at Barcelona, Spain, towards the end of the fourteenth century and died in 1432. This encyclopedia entry notes that from 1430 until his death he taught theology, philosophy and medicine at the University of Toulouse. He apparently wrote several works on theology and philosophy, but only one survives, the Theologia Naturalis. It was first written in Spanish, then translated into French by Montaigne at Paris in 1569, and into Latin at various times.

Latin editions appeared at Deventer in 1487, Strasburg in 1496, Paris in 1509 and Venice in 1581. Montaigne testifies to the great popularity the work enjoyed in his day. It represents a phase of decadent Scholasticism, defending a view that overturns the basic rule of the Scholastic method. Where thirteenth-century Schoolmen held that theology and philosophy cannot contradict each other, Sabunde's tendency runs towards the rationalistic theosophy of Raymond Lully, the entry concludes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rusicade:
Rusicade is a titular see of Numidia, mentioned by Ptolemy, Mela, Pliny, the Antonine Itinerary, and the Peutinger Table. Nothing is known of its history. Near the Thapsus mouth, it worked as Cirta's trading port, shipping grain to Rome. Its port, Stora or Ustura, held granaries built under Valentinian and Valens, still visible as ruins. The city bore the name Colonia Veneria Rusicada.

The French rebuilt it as Philippeville after it had fallen into total ruin. The town, capital of the Constantine province, has 21,550 inhabitants: 8,200 French, 5,900 foreigners, 450 Jews, and 7,000 Arabs. The ancient name survives in Ras Skidda, a point of Djebel Addouna. Commerce is considerable. Ruins of a theatre, museum, sarcophagus, inscriptions, and a basilica to Saint Digna may be found there. Six bishops are known: Verulus, Victor, Navigius, Faustinianus, Quintilianus, and Eusebius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-claude:
The Diocese of Saint-Claude comprised in the eighteenth century only twenty-six parishes, previously subject to its abbey. By the Concordat of 1802 its territory went to Besancon. The Concordat of 1817 re-erected the diocese, giving it the Jura department. The Abbey of Saint-Claude, the diocese's cradle, was one of the Christian world's great abbeys.

Between 425 and 430 the hermits Romanus and Lupic withdrew into the desert Condat, founding its monastery. Other monks joined them, land was cleared, and three new monasteries arose. These were Lauconne, La Balme, and Romainmoutier in the Canton of Vaud. After Romanus died about 460 and Lupicinus about 480, abbots followed in long line. Its first rule, drawn up between 510 and 515, later gave way to St Benedict's rule. Flourishing schools arose around Condat, producing Romanus, Archbishop of Reims, and Viventiolus, Archbishop of Lyons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-helen-o:
Helen of Sköfde was a Swedish martyr of the first half of the twelfth century. She is believed to be the daughter of the Jarl Guthorm, and her feast is kept on 31 July. Widowed young, she spent her life in charity and piety, kept her gates open to the needy, and paid for nearly the whole church of Sköfde. Her daughter's husband, a cruel man, was killed by his own servants, who falsely claimed Helen had put them up to it.

She had gone on pilgrimage to the Holy Land. Coming home, she was slain at Gothene in 1160 by her husband's kin. Buried at Sköfde, she was honoured for cures at her intercession, and in 1164 Pope Alexander III had her name entered among the canonized saints. Her well and tomb at Tiisvilde in Denmark drew pilgrims for centuries, even after the Reformation spread through Sweden.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sao-thiago-de:
São Thiago de Cabo Verde, a diocese seated on São Nicolau island, covers the Cape Verde archipelago and Portuguese Guinea on the Senegambia coast. Each province has its own governor named by Lisbon. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia maps an island diocese across two groups.

Cape Verde province, governed from Praia on São Thiago island, lies between 14 and 17 degrees north and 22 and 25 degrees west of Greenwich. Ten islands form two groups: Barlavento, with Boa Vista, Sal, São Nicolau, Santa Luzia, São Vicente, and Santo Antão, and Sotavento, with Maio, São Thiago, Fogo, and Brava. Barlavento holds two judicial districts, at Santo Antão and Mindelo, while Sotavento forms one.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-shrovetide:
Shrovetide is the English name for what most of southern Europe calls Carnival, a word the entry derives from the taking away of flesh that marked Lent's start. The English term comes from to shrive, to hear confessions. An Anglo-Saxon rule translated by Abbot Aelfric about the year 1000 ordered everyone, in the week before Lent, to go to his confessor. There he confessed his deeds and was shriven as his deeds required.

In the name itself the religious idea stands foremost, as it does in the German Fastnacht, the eve of the fast. Before a long season of deprivation, human nature allows itself some exceptional license in frolic and good cheer. The entry sees no need to appeal to vague traces of older pagan customs. One puzzle remains: the wide habit of counting the preceding Thursday, Fat Thursday, along with the Monday and Tuesday after Quinquagesima.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-richard-b:
Richard Bulstrode, soldier, diplomatist, and author born in 1610, died in 1711. Second son of Edward Bulstrode, he was schooled at Pembroke College, Cambridge, where he wrote a poem on the Duke of York's birth. In the Civil War he stayed loyal to the king, serving in the Prince of Wales's regiment, rising to Adjutant-General of Horse and then Quartermaster-General.

After a short imprisonment ended by Charles II's payment of the debt, he returned, audited a Scottish regiment in the Netherlands, and in 1673 became agent at Bruges. Recalled two years later, he was knighted in 1675 and sent to Brussels as resident until James II's accession made him envoy. When the 1688 revolution drove James to Saint-Germain, Bulstrode followed him and remained there, writing memoirs of Charles I and Charles II and a life of James II.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-adelaide:
St. Adelaide was a tenth-century abbess, dead at Cologne on 5 February 1015, and this entry follows a daughter of the nobility through two foundations. Daughter of Megingoz, Count of Guelders, she entered the convent of St. Ursula in Cologne while very young, under the Rule of St. Jerome, then became abbess of Villich, founded by her parents across the Rhine from Bonn, where she replaced Jerome's rule with Benedict's stricter one.

Her fame for holiness and miracles drew Archbishop Herbert of Cologne, who wanted her for St. Mary's convent after her sister Bertha's death, and only Emperor Otto III's command persuaded her to accept. She held both abbacies at once, died at Cologne, and was buried at Villich, where her feast is still kept.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bathilde:
St. Bathilde, or Batilde, was wife of Clovis II, king of France. This entry follows a woman whose time and place of birth are unknown, and who died in January 680. Some chronicles make her come from England and descend from Anglo-Saxon kings, but that is doubtful. Certainly she was a slave serving Erchinoald's wife — Erchinoald was mayor of the palace of Neustria.

Her unusual qualities of mind and her virtues won her master's confidence. He gave many household affairs into her charge, and after his wife's death wished to marry her. At that the young girl fled, returning only after Erchinoald had married again. About this time Clovis II met her at the mayor's house, was impressed by her beauty, grace, and good report, freed her, and married her in 649. That sudden elevation only gave her virtues new lustre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-frideswide:
Frideswide, virgin patroness of Oxford, refused a Mercian king and founded the house that became the university's shrine. Child of King Didan and Safrida, raised to holiness by Algiva, she lived about 650 to 735. When King Algar pressed his suit, she fled to Oxford, and a mysterious blindness fell on her pursuer, who left her in her cell. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death to 19 October, her principal feast.

From her cell grew a monastery where she died and was buried. Her earliest surviving life came four hundred years later, yet the entry judges the tradition's substance credible. After her translation in 1180 to a great shrine, students from all parts processed there twice yearly. Cardinal Wolsey later transformed her house, but Oxford's patroness kept her place at the city's heart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-mechtilde:
Mechtilde of Hackeborn, a Benedictine nun of Helfta in Saxony, became one of medieval Germany's great mystics. Born in 1240 or 1241 to a powerful Thuringian family, she entered the convent as a child. She won charge of the school and the choir, and used a beautiful voice to lead solemn chant. In 1261 she took charge of a five-year-old newcomer who grew into Gertrude the Great.

Christ reportedly called her his nightingale, and learned Dominicans sought her counsel. Only in her fiftieth year did she learn that two nuns had written down her revelations, with Gertrude nearly finishing the book. After prayer she corrected the manuscript herself, and it spread as the Book of Special Grace. She died at Helfta on 19 November 1298, and her feast is kept in late February.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-winefride:
Winefride, a Welsh virgin martyr, was beheaded for refusing a prince and restored to life by Beuno, tradition says. Born at Holywell about 600 to Thevit, a Cambrian magnate of three Flintshire manors, and Wenlo, sister of Beuno, she grew up hearing Beuno preach. At fifteen she gave herself to devotion and austerity, passing whole nights watching in church.

When the prince Caradog demanded her, she fled toward Beuno's chapel, and he struck off her head. Beuno restored her, the legend says, and a spring burst where her head fell, the famous Holywell. She later ruled a convent at Gwytherin. The entry traces the legend, the well's pilgrimage, and the relics' history with care for sources. She died at Gwytherin on 3 November 660, honoured as Wales's beloved virgin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-suicide:
Suicide, the act of causing one's own death, is treated here under three heads: its notions and divisions, the moral principles for judging it, and statistics on its frequency. Death may be caused directly, by a mortal wound, or by omission, such as refusing to leave a burning house. Direct suicide intends death as an end or a means, like escaping disgrace.

Indirect suicide, a name rarely used, covers acts that bring death without intending it, such as nursing plague victims knowing the task will kill the nurse. Catholic teaching calls positive direct suicide without God's consent a grave wrong, since God alone owns life outright, while man holds only its use, charged to guard it. Closing sections gather nineteenth-century figures and weigh their explanations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-venerable:
England's historian and Doctor of the Church, Bede, tells his own life in this entry's frame, born in 672 or 673 and dying in 735. His Ecclesiastical History of the English People closes with an autobiographical chapter, practically all we know of him, written in 731 as death drew near. Simplicity and piety mark every line, the entry notes, and light falls on how the great work was composed.

Baeda, servant of Christ and priest of Wearmouth and Jarrow's monastery of Peter and Paul, gathered his history from ancient documents, elders' traditions, and his own knowledge, with the Lord's help. Given at seven to Abbot Benedict Biscop's care, he spent his life in study, teaching, and writing. Works, chronology, and fame complete the portrait.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodore-coel:
Franciscan Theodore Coelde of Münster won fame as the plague priest of Brussels. Born at Münster in 1435, he died at Louvain on 11 December 1515. He is not the Dominican Theodore of Münster nor the Augustinian Theodore of Osnabrück, names drawn from his birth town and his father's town. Cologne schooled him, Augustinian hermits took him young, and Franciscans took him in the Netherlands in 1454.

When plague struck Brussels in 1489, he walked the streets giving last rites to the dying. His sacristan fell ill, so Coelde hung a lamp from his belt and carried pyx and bell in his hands. More than thirty-two thousand souls got last rites from him ere plague passed. A short, plain catechism he wrote in 1470 spread his name still further.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-pounde:
Thomas Pounde, a Jesuit lay brother born at Beaumond, Hampshire, in 1538, spent much of his life in prison for his faith. Eldest son of William Pounde, he entered Lincoln's Inn in 1559 and became esquire of the body to Queen Elizabeth, even playing Mercury in a masque at Kenilworth in 1565. A public slight from the queen at Christmas helped turn him from court life.

Reconciled to the Catholic Church, he began work as a proselytizer and paid for it with years in the Marshalsea, Winchester Gaol, Wisbech, the Tower and other prisons. Made a Jesuit lay brother in 1578, he kept his faith through nearly a decade at Wisbech and further terms in the Tower. He died at Beaumond in February 1613.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tyrannicide:
Tyrannicide means the killing of a tyrant, usually by a private person for the common good. This entry examines when, if ever, Catholic moral teaching allows it. It draws a sharp line between two kinds of tyrant. One is the usurper who seizes power unjustly. The other is the lawful ruler who turns his power to oppression. Each case raises questions about lawful authority, self-defence, and enduring hardship rather than taking up the sword.

The survey runs through the authorities, from John of Salisbury in the twelfth century to the Jesuit Mariana. Mariana allowed killing only after warning and public judgment had failed. It records the Council of Constance's condemnation in 1415 of a sweeping licence to kill any tyrant. It also covers later writers who allowed passive resistance and, in extreme cases, active defence. Reformers such as Luther, Melanchthon, and Knox appear for contrast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-victor-de-lap:
Victor de Laprade was a French poet and critic who lived from 1812 to 1883. He studied medicine, then law, was admitted to the bar, but soon left it to teach French literature at Lyons. Losing that chair in 1863 for publishing Les Muses d'État, a satire on the Second Empire's men, and thereafter devoting himself entirely to poetry.

In 1858 he had taken Musset's seat in the French Academy. Probably the most idealistic French poet of his century, in talent somewhat resembling Lamartine, his acknowledged master, he sang God, nature, fatherland, mankind, friendship, and family in lofty, harmonious verse. His early, impersonal phase joins ancient myth to Christianity in Psyché, Odes et Poèmes, Poèmes évangéliques, and Symphonies. Les Idylles héroïques of 1858 marks a turn toward a more Christian and humane second phase, shedding earlier poetic pantheism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vincent-de-va:
Vincent de Valverde was a Spanish Dominican, first Bishop of Cuzco, who died at Puná Island near Guayaquil in 1541. Born at Oropesa toward the close of the fifteenth century, related to Pizarro and Cortés, he professed at San Esteban, Salamanca, in 1524. In 1529 accompanied Pizarro as missionary on the voyage to conquer Peru.

Before Cajamarca in November 1532 he sought Atahualpa's peaceful submission, then instructed and baptized the unfortunate Inca king. Named by Charles V as first Bishop of Cuzco and confirmed by Paul III in 1537, he also served as Protector of the Natives. A charge that forced him constantly to cross the rude soldiery, who showed the Indians neither justice nor mercy. After settling, in vain, the feud between Almagro and Pizarro, and fleeing after Pizarro's assassination, he was killed by Indians at Puná.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vinzenz-eduar:
Vinzenz Eduard Milde was Prince-Archbishop of Vienna, born at Brünn in Moravia in 1777 and dying at Vienna in 1853. His monument in St Stephen's Cathedral portrays, under the words charity and prayer, a catechist bending over two children and a priest elevating the Blessed Sacrament. Its inscription says charity and prayer link together the inhabitants of this world and those of the next. It witnesses to Milde's fame as catechist and founder of a seminary for priests and teachers. Against his stepfather's opposition and with his mother's support, poor and friendless, he entered Vienna's little seminary in 1794. Befriending future church historian Vinzenz Darnaut and future bishop Jakob Frint, with whom he later served as court chaplain.

He became catechist in the Normal High School, successor to the famous Augustin Gruber, and holder of the university chair of pedagogy, before rising to the archbishopric.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-walther-von-d:
Walther von der Vogelweide was a medieval German lyric poet, a Minnesinger, born about 1170 and dying in 1228. Only one old document names him, a record of Bishop Wolfger of Passau's travelling expenses noting five solidi for a fur coat given to the singer on 12 November 1203. His birthplace rests on conjecture from his poems, above all two in imperfect rhyme, explicable, since he was elsewhere exact in rhyme, only by Bavarian-Austrian dialect.

Austria is therefore probably his native land. His songs cannot be ordered chronologically with certainty, so they cannot be read against his life. His certain merit is developing knightly Minne poetry artistically and introducing the true love song into court poetry, alongside didactic verse the entry goes on to discuss.
cousin-maude:
Mary J. Holmes set her novel Cousin Maude among the northern hills of New England, where a young widow faces a risky second marriage. Matilda Remington, widowed early and short of money, agrees to wed Dr. Kennedy, a rich, cold, self-pleased suitor. He arrives on foot from the depot, too careful with cash to hire a ride. Housekeeper Janet distrusts him at first sight.

Holmes follows Matilda into the doctor's grand home, Laurel Hill, and into a household ruled by pride. Little Louis, the motherless boy who needs care, gives the marriage its tender center. Chapters trace rival engagements, a dark hour of trouble, a blind girl, and two bridal nights that contrast sharply. Maude Glendower, the cousin of the title, enters late and shifts the family's fortunes. Sentimental fiction fans find the Holmes formula here: love, money, pride, and patience tested inside one country household.
dickory-cronke-the-dumb-philosopher-or-g:
Daniel Defoe's Dickory Cronke, The Dumb Philosopher, from the 1889 Bell edition, claims to extract its account from the Cornish tinner's own papers. Dickory, born dumb, kept silence for fifty-eight years, then gained speech a few days before death. The title page promises his life, his declaration of faith, his meditations, and his prophecies for Europe from 1720 to 1729.

The narrative explains his dumbness as a strange fit that left and returned without pain, sending him back to his pen in his original state. Whether Defoe invented or edited Cronke remains disputed. The little book mixes wonder biography, devotional meditation, and political prophecy in the manner Defoe could produce faster than any man in London.

down-the-mother-lode:
Vivia Hemphill collected Down the Mother Lode as pioneer tales of California, copyrighted in 1922. Her foreword explains the Mother Lode as the great gold-bearing belt running through the Sierra foothills. Geologists, engineers, and old miners each define it differently in her pages. Hemphill says every tale rests on a real incident from the gold era.

Hemphill gathered the material from a passing generation of old-timers. She aimed to entertain first and inform second, by her own admission. flood-tide:
Bassett sets a love tale in a Cape Cod village in Flood Tide, dated 1921. Sara Ware Bassett peoples her story with Willie, Delight, Tiny, and Robert Morton. The chapter heads promise village weather of the heart: the green-eyed monster, an apparition, a second spirit, and shadows, with a conspiracy to come.

The sampled talk turns on a belt and buckle. Madam Lee teases Robert Morton, who she says is chained in a sleepy village. Cynthia came back from Wilton in a wretched humor, and her spirit when asked about her buckle told Madam Lee all she needed. The buckle, Robert owns at last, belongs to a girl. Bassett writes of courtship and gossip in a small place, where a lost buckle can carry a whole plot.
fortitude:
Walpole builds Peter Westcott's story in four books, from Scaw House to a London bookshop and back. The Cornish household debates the boy Peter over the dark shop of Zachary Tan. School at Dawson's proves a gate into hell rather than into life.

Grown and poor in London, Peter writes at a penny bottle of ink in an exercise book. In a fortnight he finishes an essay, The Sea Road, owing much to Stevenson, and three stories. He means to advance once more to the attack on editors. Hugh Walpole published Fortitude in 1913 and dedicated it to Charles Maude, his most honest critic.

Martin Heidegger gave a lecture course in 1925 on the history of the concept of time. In it he traces how thinkers from Aristotle through Augustine to the modern age understood time, and where each account fell short.

The course laid groundwork for Being and Time, the book that made Heidegger famous two years later. It remains a landmark of twentieth-century philosophy, and the full text lets readers follow the lectures session by session, from Greek physics to the structure of human existence.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Al:
